3. Walashahi was the emperor's bodyguard.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
133.x: All three are correct: chehra was the descriptive roll, Akbar revived dagh and chehra, and walashahi was the bodyguard.

133.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Mughal central ministers?
o: Wazir or Diwan – finance and revenue
Mir Bakhshi – military pay, mansabs and intelligence
Mir Saman – religion, charity and madad-i-maash grants
Sadr-us-Sudur – religion, charity and madad-i-maash grants
133.x: The Mir Saman supervised the royal household and karkhanas; religion and charity were under the Sadr-us-Sudur.

133.s: What did the authority of the Wakil largely become under Akbar?
133.x: Although the Wakil had traditionally been the chief adviser or regent, the office became largely symbolic under Akbar.
133.tq: Test the change in the practical importance of a central office.
xs: Under Akbar the **Wakil's** authority became largely **symbolic** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The Wakil (vakil-us-saltanat) was chief adviser/regent; **Bairam Khan** held it in the regency, after which Akbar reduced it.
xa: Real finance power passed to the **Wazir/Diwan**.
Military power lay with the **Mir Bakhshi**.
Sultanate ministries (**Wazir**, **Diwan-i-Arz**) fed the Mughal model.

133.s: Under which official did Mughal intelligence, run through waqia-navis, khufia-navis and harkaras, come?
133.x: Intelligence was under the Mir Bakhshi.
xa: The Mir Bakhshi also ran **recruitment, pay and musters**.
**Muhtasib** = public morals.
**Mustaufi** = auditor.

133.s: Which Mughal central official supervised the royal household and the karkhanas?
133.x: The Mir Saman supervised the royal household and karkhanas.

133.s: Who was the Mughal chief justice who administered the Sharia?
133.x: The Qazi-ul-Quzat was the chief justice under the Sharia.

133.s: Who were the 'waqia-navis' in the Mughal espionage system?
133.x: Waqia-navis were news-writers; khufia-navis wrote secret reports and harkaras were runners/spies.

133.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Tashiha — verification and muster of troops and horses
Chehra — descriptive roll of a trooper
Dagh — preparation of revenue papers by the assistant to the amalguzar
133.x: Dagh was the branding of horses to prevent substitution. Preparation of revenue papers and accounts was the duty of the Bitikchi.
133.tq: Find the one pair that belongs to a different administrative function.
xs: **Dagh — preparing revenue papers** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Dagh** was the **branding of horses** to stop substitution.
The others are right: **Tashiha** = muster/verification; **Chehra** = descriptive roll of a trooper.
xa: Dagh was used earlier by **Alauddin** and **Sher Shah**.
Failure to present the required sawars at musters → **pay cuts**.
Musters were held under the **Mir Bakhshi**.

133.s: Which one of the following pairs of term and meaning is not correctly matched?
o: Khalisa – Villages whose income went directly to the state treasury.
Inam – Land allotted to learned and religious man
Jagir – Territorial assignment given to Mansabdars in lieu of salary.
133.x: Mauza means a village, not rebellious territory (that was mawas), so this pair is wrong. Khalisa (crown land), inam (grant to learned men) and jagir (in lieu of salary) are correct.

133.s: Which of the following contributed to the decline of the Mughal Empire after Aurangzeb?
o: Loss of Bengal to the Marathas
133.x: The jagir crisis, along with the Deccan wars and Rajput alienation, contributed to the decline.
xa: The Deccan war **drained the treasury**; Aurangzeb died there in **1707**.
Rajput revolt: **Marwar and Mewar** under **Durgadas Rathore**.
Aurangzeb spent his last **25** years in the Deccan.

133.s: What were madad-i-maash grants generally?
o: Transferable assignments made to cavalrymen in lieu of salary
Crown lands reserved for the imperial treasury
Revenue-free grants to scholars and religious men under the Sadr
133.x: Madad-i-maash consisted of revenue-free grants to scholars and religious men and was administered under the Sadr.
133.tq: Identify the beneficiary and administrative authority associated with the grant.
xs: **Madad-i-maash** = **revenue-free grants** to scholars and religious men, under the **Sadr** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Grants in lieu of salary were **Tankhwah** jagirs; crown land was **Khalisa**; hereditary Rajput grants were **Watan** jagirs.
xa: The **Sadr-us-Sudur** handled religion, charity and religious endowments.
He also appointed **qazis**.
**Altamgha** = perpetual grant.

133.s: What was a perpetual Mughal jagir grant called?
133.x: Altamgha was perpetual; Tankhwah was in lieu of salary, Watan hereditary in the homeland and Mashrut conditional.
xa: **In'am** jagir was free of any service obligation.
⚠ **Tankhwah** = transferable; **Watan** = hereditary, not transferred.
**Khalisa** was crown land, not a jagir.

133.s: What was a Watan jagir?
o: The hereditary home territory of a zamindar or Rajput chief
A grant in lieu of salary
A grant subject to conditions of service
133.x: Watan jagirs were hereditary home territories and were not transferred by the state.
xa: **Tankhwah** (Tankha) jagirs were **transferable**, given in lieu of salary.
**Altamgha** = perpetual grant; **In'am** = free of service.
Transfers came about every **3-4** years.

133.s: Which of the following was NOT a jagir in the Mughal system?
133.x: Khalisa was crown land, not a jagir; tankhwah, watan and in'am were jagir types.

133.s: What was a Mughal jagir granted free of any service obligation called?
133.x: In'am was free of service; tankhwah was in lieu of salary and mashrut was conditional.

133.s: Why were Mughal jagirs frequently transferred, generally after about three to four years?
o: To convert all jagirs into Khalisa lands
To make them hereditary among local chiefs
To prevent mansabdars from developing local roots and becoming independent feudal lords
To ensure that peasants elected their revenue collectors
133.x: Frequent transfers, usually every three to four years, were intended to prevent mansabdars from establishing local bases and becoming independent feudal lords.
133.tq: Link the numerical interval with the administrative purpose rather than treating it as an isolated figure.
xs: Jagirs were transferred every **3-4** years to **stop mansabdars striking local roots** and becoming **independent feudal lords** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Transfers kept jagirs **non-hereditary**; they did not convert them to khalisa.
xa: Side effect: short-term jagirdars **squeezed peasants**.
**Bejagiri** (waiting without jagirs) bred discontent and faction.
The mansab-jagir system **bound the nobility to the emperor**.

133.s: What does the term 'bejagiri' refer to?
o: Mansabdars were kept waiting without jagirs
Mansabdars were appointed as village accountants
Revenue was transferred directly to the imperial treasury
Jagirs became hereditary in the home territories of chiefs
133.x: Bejagiri meant that mansabdars remained without jagir assignments. It bred discontent and factionalism at the imperial court.
133.tq: Discriminate between a condition of non-assignment and the normal jagir arrangement.
xs: **Bejagiri** = mansabdars **kept waiting without jagirs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It led to **discontent and faction** at court.
Revenue going straight to the treasury came from **khalisa**; hereditary homeland grants were **Watan** jagirs.
xa: Under **Aurangzeb**, mansabdars grew while **paibaqi** shrank.
**Satish Chandra**: shortage of jagirs relative to claimants.
**Athar Ali**: influx of **Deccani and Maratha** nobles.

133.s: Which of the following explains the jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb?
o: Reduction of nobility through the exclusion of Deccani and Maratha nobles
Growth in mansabdars, shrinkage of good jagirs and increasing pressure on peasants
Decline in mansabdars, expansion of profitable land and relief to peasants
Abolition of jagirs and complete transfer of revenue collection to village panchayats
133.x: Under Aurangzeb, the number of mansabdars increased, profitable jagirs became scarce, and peasants were subjected to intensified extraction.
133.tq: Combine the linked causes and effects instead of treating them as isolated facts.
xs: **Growth in mansabdars**, **shrinkage of good jagirs** and **pressure on peasants** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under **Aurangzeb**, paying land for assignment (**paibaqi**) shrank as claimants grew.
Deccani and Maratha nobles were **added**, not excluded (**Athar Ali**).
xa: Result: ruthless extraction, **agrarian ruin**, decline.
⚠ **Irfan Habib** = agrarian crisis; **Satish Chandra** = jagir shortage.
The crisis is a **core explanation of Mughal decline**.

133.s: The breakdown of which system is regarded as a core explanation of the decline of the Mughal Empire?
133.x: The breakdown of the jagirdari system, known as the jagirdari crisis, is a core explanation of Mughal decline.
xa: Crisis: mansabdars grew while **paibaqi** shrank under **Aurangzeb**.
Qutb Shahi Golconda officials: **Mir Jumla** (finance), **Ain-ul-Mulk** (military), **Majumdar** (auditor).
Golconda village officials: **Mukaddam** and **Kulkarni**.

133.s: Which historian explained the Mughal jagirdari crisis as a shortage of jagirs relative to claimants?
133.x: Satish Chandra stressed the shortage of jagirs; Irfan Habib the agrarian crisis; Athar Ali the influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles.
xa: Revolts in Habib's view: **Jat**, **Satnami**, **Maratha**.
The crisis arose under **Aurangzeb** as **paibaqi** shrank.
The jagirdari breakdown is the **core explanation of Mughal decline**.

133.s: Which of the following states retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration?
o: Qutb Shahi state of Golconda only
133.x: The Asaf Jahi state of Hyderabad retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration.
133.tq: Use the regional application angle to identify the state associated with the administrative practice.
xs: The **Asaf Jahi** state of **Hyderabad** kept a Mughal-style **jagirdari** administration — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Kakatiya **Nayankara** is only compared with the jagir; Golconda's set-up was Qutb Shahi (Peshwa, Mir Jumla, Ain-ul-Mulk, Majumdar).
xa: Qutb Shahi officials: **Mir Jumla** (finance), **Ain-ul-Mulk** (military), **Majumdar** (auditor).
Under Tana Shah, Golconda had **37 sarkars and 517 parganas**.
The jagirdari breakdown is the **core explanation of Mughal decline**.

133.s: Which historian explained the jagirdari crisis as an agrarian crisis?
133.x: Irfan Habib saw it as an agrarian crisis; Satish Chandra stressed a shortage of jagirs.

133.s: To what did Athar Ali mainly link the jagirdari crisis?
o: The influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles
133.x: Athar Ali stressed the influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles under Aurangzeb.

133.s: Under Aurangzeb, what was the pool of land held back for assignment as jagirs, which proved too small for the growing number of mansabdars, called?
133.x: Paibaqi was land kept unassigned, available for allotment as jagirs; under Aurangzeb more mansabdars and too little good paibaqi land squeezed the peasants. Khalisa was crown land, Altamgha a hereditary grant and Watan a hereditary home jagir.

134.s: The term 'Chakla' has been used in Medieval Indian History sources. This was
o: Territorial unit between Subah and Paragnah, but not
134.x: Chakla was a unit between the subah and the pargana but not identical with the sarkar; it was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.

134.s: With reference to medieval India, which one of the following is the correct sequence in ascending order in terms of size?
134.x: Ascending by size: pargana, then sarkar, then suba (province).

134.s: What was ‘district’ known as during the Mughal administration?
134.x: Under the Mughals the district was the sarkar; the suba was the province and the pargana the sub-district.

134.s: How many subahs were there by the end of Akbar's reign?
134.x: Akbar had 12 subahs in 1580 and 15 by the end of his reign; Aurangzeb had 21.
xa: The **Subahdar** handled law and order; the provincial **Diwan** handled revenue.
The subah also had a **Bakhshi**, **Sadr** and **Qazi**.
⚠ **Chakla** sits between pargana and sarkar.

134.s: Above which unit did the pargana stand immediately in the Mughal administrative hierarchy?
134.x: The order from lowest to highest was village, pargana, sarkar and subah, so the pargana stood just above the village.

134.s: Which of the following is the correct ascending order of Mughal administrative units?
134.x: From smallest to largest the units were village, pargana, sarkar and subah (province).

134.s: Besides the Faujdar, who was the principal official of a Mughal Sarkar?
134.x: A Sarkar was run by the Faujdar and Amalguzar; a Suba by the Subedar and provincial Diwan.
xa: **Pargana** (tehsil): **Shiqdar** + amil, qanungo, chaudhari.
The Mughal **"district"** = **Sarkar**.
The **Diwan** was independent of the Subedar — a check on him.

134.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Chakla is correct?
o: It was a unit between the Suba and Pargana and was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.
It was a military rank assigned to a Mansabdar.
It was identical with the Sarkar in every province.
It was the smallest village-level revenue unit.
134.x: Chakla was a unit between the Suba and Pargana, but it was not identical with the Sarkar. It was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.
134.tq: Separate the similar territorial terms Chakla and Sarkar by their exact position in the hierarchy.
xs: The **Chakla** was a unit **between suba and pargana**, prominent in **Bengal** under **Murshid Quli Khan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ It was **not identical** to the sarkar (PYQ).
It was an administrative unit, not a military rank or village unit.
xa: Ascending order: **Pargana - Sarkar - Suba** (UPSC **2021**).
Akbar started with **12** subas; Aurangzeb had **21**.
The state's reach effectively ended at the **pargana**.

134.s: At which level did the effective reach of Mughal rural administration generally end?
134.x: The state's effective reach ended at the Pargana; villages were largely self-governing.
xa: Village: **Muqaddam**, **patwari**, **chowkidar**, panchayat.
Pargana (tehsil): **Shiqdar** + amil, **qanungo**, chaudhari.
⚠ **Patwari** = village accountant; **Muqaddam** = village headman.

134.s: How many subas did the Mughal empire have under Aurangzeb?
134.x: Akbar began with 12 and had 15 by the end of his reign; Aurangzeb had 21, Golconda being the 21st.

134.s: Under whom was the Chakla, a unit not identical with the sarkar, prominent in Bengal?
134.x: The chakla was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.

134.s: The meaning of word Bantai during the Medieval period was?
134.x: Batai (bantai, ghallabakhshi) was a system of calculating revenue by sharing the actual crop between the state and the peasant, not a religious, wealth or property tax.

134.s: Which one of the following statements is not true about Ijarah system?
o: It was a system of revenue farming.
It encouraged the role of middlemen
under this system, land revenue was fixed for the peasant.
The ijaradar paid a fixed amount to the state treasury.
134.x: Under ijarah, revenue was farmed out to an ijaradar who paid a fixed sum to the treasury and squeezed the peasant, so the peasant's revenue was not fixed. Statements (a), (b) and (d) are true.

134.s: Who formalised the Dahsala settlement of 1580?
134.x: Raja Todar Mal formalised the zabt system as the Dahsala settlement in 1580.

134.s: Under the Dahsala system, revenue was fixed on the average yield of how many past years?
134.x: Dahsala rates were based on the average yield of the past ten years, payable in cash.

134.s: In which regions was Nasaq, an estimate based on past assessments, mainly used?
134.x: Nasaq was used in Bengal and Orissa.

134.s: Which Mughal revenue system was based on sharing of the crop?
134.x: Batai (ghallabakhshi or bhaoli) shared the crop; kankut estimated the crop.

134.s: Which Mughal revenue system was based on an estimate of the crop?
134.x: Kankut fixed revenue by estimating the standing crop; batai was crop-sharing.

134.s: In Akbar's land classification, what was land cultivated every year called?
134.x: Polaj land was cultivated every year; parauti was left fallow for a short time.

134.s: How was land left uncultivated for five years or more classed?
134.x: Banjar land lay uncultivated 5 years or more; chachar lay fallow 3–4 years.

134.s: Who amongst the following is a land record officer?
134.x: The Patwari was the village accountant who kept the land records. Lambardar and Zaildar were village headmen in colonial Punjab, and the zamindar held revenue rights.

134.s: In a Mughal province, which official managed revenue and acted as an independent check on the governor?
134.x: The provincial Diwan managed revenue and checked the Subahdar, who handled governance and law and order.
xa: Other subah officials: **Bakhshi**, **Sadr**, **Qazi**.
Pargana: **Shiqdar** (military/police).
Village: **Muqaddam**, **Patwari**.

134.s: Who kept land records and revenue papers in a Mughal sarkar?
134.x: The Bitikchi kept land records and revenue papers; the Khazanadar was the treasurer.

134.s: Who was the head of the patwaris at the pargana level?
134.x: The Qanungo headed the patwaris and kept records; the Karkun was a clerk.

134.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
134.x: The Kotwal handled town police and markets; the Shiqdar was the pargana executive and the Khazanadar the treasurer.

134.s: Who was in charge of military command and law and order in a Mughal sarkar?
134.x: The faujdar headed the sarkar's military and kept law and order; the kotwal policed towns.

134.s: Who was the executive and police officer at the pargana level in Mughal administration?
134.x: The Shiqdar headed the executive and police work of a pargana; the Faujdar worked at the sarkar level.

134.s: Who was the village accountant in Mughal administration?
134.x: The Patwari was the village accountant; the Qanungo was head of the patwaris at pargana level.

134.s: Why was the provincial Diwan in the Mughal administration independent of the Subedar?
o: controlled the city police and markets
served as a check on the Subedar in revenue and finance
134.x: The provincial Diwan handled revenue and finance independently of the Subedar, thereby acting as a check on the governor.
134.tq: Ask which official performed the balancing or checking function rather than the executive function.
xs: The provincial **Diwan**, handling **revenue and finance**, was **independent of the subedar** — a **check** on him — so option **(3)** is correct.
Military command lay with the **Subedar**/**Faujdar**; city police with the **Kotwal**.
xa: The **Subedar** (sipahsalar/nazim) kept law and order and enforced imperial decrees.
Subedar-diwan separation + **zabti** = model for later revenue administration.
⚠ The British **district collector** combined powers the Mughals kept apart.

134.s: Which Mughal city official was in charge of police, markets and a watch on newcomers?
134.x: The Kotwal was the city police chief who also controlled markets and watched newcomers.

134.s: In Mughal provincial administration, what did the Diwan-i-Tan deal with?
134.x: The Diwan-i-Tan handled salaries (tankhwah) and jagir assignments.

134.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
134.x: The Muhtasib looked after public morals; the Bakhshi handled military pay and musters.

134.s: By which other name was the Subedar, the governor of a Mughal suba, known?
134.x: The Subedar, governor of a suba, was also called Nazim or Sipahsalar.

134.s: Which of the following pairs (Official – Duty) is correctly matched?
134.x: The Potdar was the treasurer. The Bitikchi prepared assessment and land records, the Qanungo kept pargana-level records and the Patwari was the village accountant.
xa: The Qanungo's post was **hereditary**.
The Bitikchi was **assistant to the amalguzar** and prepared revenue papers.
Sarkar treasurer = **khazanadar / fotadar**.

134.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Muqaddam — Village headman and revenue collector
Khazanadar — Keeper of hereditary land records
134.x: The Muqaddam, or Patel, was the village headman and collected revenue. The Khazanadar or Fotadar was the treasurer at the Sarkar level.
134.tq: Check whether the official is placed at the correct administrative level before accepting the duty.
xs: **Muqaddam — village headman and revenue collector** is correctly matched — so option **(2)** is correct.
The Muqaddam was also called **patel**.
**Bitikchi** was an accountant; **Khazanadar** a **treasurer**; the **Qanungo** kept **land records** at the pargana.
xa: The **Kotwal** was the city police chief.
**Patwari** = village accountant.
Qutb Shahi Golconda's village headman: **mukaddam**.

134.s: In a Mughal sarkar, what was the role of the Potdar or Khazanadar?
134.x: The Potdar (Khazanadar/Fotadar) was the sarkar treasurer; the Bitikchi was the accountant.

134.s: Who was the official responsible for collecting revenue in charge of a district?
134.x: The amalguzar, also called amil, was the district-level revenue collector.
134.tq: Match the official with the level and function of revenue administration.
xs: The **Amalguzar** (amil) was the **revenue collector in charge of a district** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
**Karkun** = pargana clerk-writer; **Potdar** = treasurer; **Bitikchi** = accountant.
xa: ⚠ **Amalguzar** = collector; **Bitikchi** = accountant; **Potdar** = treasurer — all sarkar level.
**Karori** = collector of a circle yielding **one crore dams**.
**Chaudhari** = pargana revenue collector (local notable).

134.s: Who was the Mughal village headman who also collected revenue?
134.x: The Muqaddam (Patel) was the village headman; the Patwari was the village accountant.

134.s:
With reference to Mughal India, what is / are the difference / differences between Jagirdar and Zamindar?

A. Jagirdars were holders of land assignments in lieu of judicial and police duties, whereas Zamindars were holders of revenue rights without obligation to perform any duty other than revenue collection.

B. Land assignments to Jagirdars were hereditary and revenue rights of Zamindars were not hereditary.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
134.x: Jagirs were revenue assignments in lieu of salary, not of judicial or police duty, so A is wrong. Jagirs were not hereditary, while zamindari rights were, so B is wrong too.

134.s: In the Mughal system, in lieu of what was a jagir given to a mansabdar?
o: judicial and police duties in the area
134.x: Jagirs were revenue assignments in lieu of salary and military service; they carried no judicial or police duties (UPSC 2019 key: a statement linking jagirs to judicial/police duties is wrong). A jagir gave no ownership of land, and revenue-free grants for scholars and holy men were madad-i-maash.
134.tq: Jagir = salary + military service, not police/judicial, not ownership.
xs: A jagir was given **in lieu of salary and military service** — so option **(2)** is correct.
UPSC **2019** key: jagirs carried **no judicial/police duties**.
A jagir gave **no ownership**; revenue-free grants for religious men were **madad-i-maash**.
xa: **Tankhwah** jagirs were **transferable**.
Transfers about every **3-4** years stopped mansabdars striking **local roots**.
⚠ Zamindars held **hereditary** rights; jagirdars did not.

134.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a jagirdar from a zamindar?
o: A jagirdar held hereditary local rights, whereas a zamindar was frequently transferred
A jagirdar held a revenue assignment in lieu of salary, whereas a zamindar possessed hereditary local rights and acted as an intermediary
A zamindar was appointed only as a provincial governor, whereas a jagirdar was a village accountant
Both were hereditary proprietors of land with identical powers
134.x: A mansabdar holding a jagir had a non-hereditary right to collect revenue in lieu of salary and was frequently transferred. A zamindar held hereditary rights over land revenue and local power and acted as an intermediary between the state and peasants.
134.tq: Compare the basis of tenure, transferability and local role.
xs: A **jagirdar** held a **revenue assignment in lieu of salary**; a **zamindar** held **hereditary** rights and was a **local intermediary** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Jagirdars were **not hereditary** and **frequently transferred**; zamindars were **not transferred** by the state.
Neither was a governor or village accountant; their powers were not identical.
xa: A jagir was **not property in land**.
**Watan** jagirs of Rajput chiefs were hereditary and not transferred.
Sultanate **iqta** and Kakatiya **Nayankara** are compared with the jagir.

134.s: In which sequence was a Mansabdar paid through a tankhwah jagir connected to revenue collection?
o: Mansabdar — Tankhwah jagir — Jagirdar's agents — Zamindars — Peasant
134.x: The Mansabdar got a rank and was paid by a tankhwah jagir; the jagirdar's agents collected the assessed revenue (jama) through the zamindars, who kept a hereditary share, and the peasant paid about one-third of the produce.
134.tq: Trace the institutional flow from rank and assignment to local collection and peasant payment.
xs: **Mansabdar → tankhwah jagir → jagirdar's agents → zamindars → peasant** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The agents collected the assessed revenue (**jama**) through **zamindars**, who kept a **hereditary share**.
The peasant paid about **one-third** of produce.
xa: ⚠ Jagirdar = outsider, **not hereditary**; zamindar = local, **hereditary**.
Zamindars had armed retainers and helped **police and collection**.
Short-tenure jagirdars pressed for more → local face of the **jagirdari crisis**.

134.s: In the Mughal revenue system, the peasant generally paid approximately what share of the produce?
134.x: The peasant's payment was approximately one-third of the produce in the mansabdar-jagirdar-zamindar revenue linkage.
134.tq: Retain the approximate fraction and reject nearby conventional revenue shares.
xs: The peasant paid about **one-third** of produce — so option **(1)** is correct.
This sat at the end of the **mansabdar → jagirdar → zamindar** chain.
xa: Assessed revenue was called **jama**.
Zamindars kept a **hereditary share**.
Qutb Shahi Golconda instead **farmed out revenue by auction**.

134.s: Which of the following was a major local manifestation of the jagirdari crisis?
o: Zamindars became salaried imperial officials and peasants received remissions permanently.
The state abolished revenue collection through local intermediaries.
Short-tenure Jagirdars pressed for more revenue, zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants fled.
Jagirdars reduced demands and zamindars abandoned cultivation.
134.x: Short tenure encouraged Jagirdars to press for higher collections; Zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants sometimes fled, producing a local face of the jagirdari crisis.
134.tq: Identify the connected cause-and-effect chain rather than an isolated symptom.
xs: **Short-tenure jagirdars pressed for more**, **zamindars resisted or rebelled**, and **peasants fled** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This was the **local face of the jagirdari crisis**; jagirdars did not reduce demands.
xa: Jagirdars were transferred often and were **outsiders** to the area.
Zamindars had **armed retainers**.
UPSC **2019**: jagirs were neither for judicial/police duties nor hereditary.

134.s: In lieu of what were Mughal jagirs given as revenue assignments?
o: Salary for state, mainly military, service
134.x: Jagirs were revenue assignments in lieu of salary for state service; they were not hereditary and were often transferred.
xa: Hereditary rights belonged to **zamindars**.
The **Diwan-i-Tan** handled jagir assignments.

the gold coin used for long-distance trade
coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount

Travellers' accounts = main source for Mughal social history, read against **Persian chronicles**.

136.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Mughal urban society?
o: Artisans worked both in state karkhanas and privately.
Artisans were often organised in guilds.
Urban society consisted of merchants and soldiers only.
Physicians, teachers and lawyers formed professional groups.
136.x: Urban society was not made up only of merchants and soldiers; it also included artisans and professional groups.

136.s: Who founded the Dars-e-Nizami?
136.x: Mulla Nizamuddin of Sihali, linked with Firangi Mahal, Lucknow, founded the Dars-e-Nizami.

136.s: For what was Firangi Mahal at Lucknow noted as a madrasa?
136.x: Firangi Mahal in Lucknow was a madrasa associated with Muslim jurisprudence.
xs: **Firangi Mahal (Lucknow)** was a madrasa of **Muslim jurisprudence** — option **(2)**.
This was the UPPSC **2016** key.
xa: **Nauroz** = **Persian New Year**, adopted from the **Zoroastrians** (UPPSC **2001** key).
**Tuladan** = weighing the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday — a **Hindu** custom adopted by Akbar.

136.s: What is the name of the award given to meritorious men in the Mughal Court in the form of a Robe of Honour that was once worn by the Emperor?
136.x: The khilat was a robe of honour, a garment once worn by the emperor, given to meritorious men. The sarapa ('head to foot') was a set of tunic, turban and sash, and the padma murassa a jewelled lotus given only in exceptional cases.

136.s: Mughal adopted ‘Navroj’ festival from
136.x: Nauroz (Navroz) is the Persian New Year of the Zoroastrian (Parsi) tradition; Akbar made it a Mughal court festival and Aurangzeb stopped it. It is not a Jewish, Mongol or Turkish festival.

136.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Mughal court customs?
o: Sijda and paibos were introduced by Shah Jahan.
Jharokha darshan was begun by Akbar and ended by Aurangzeb.
Tuladan weighed the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday.
Nauroz was a Persian New Year festival adopted from the Zoroastrians.
136.x: Sijda and paibos were introduced by Akbar, not Shah Jahan.
xa: Tuladan was a **Hindu** custom adopted by Akbar; the goods were given to the poor.
Nauroz was **stopped by Aurangzeb** (UPPSC **2001** key for Zoroastrian origin).
**Qutb Shahi Golconda** also celebrated **Nauroz**.

136.s: In Qutb Shahi Golconda, by what name was Muharram popularly known?
136.x: Muharram was known as Peerla Panduga in Golconda.
xa: **Abdullah Qutb Shah**'s Hyderabad had **20,000** registered prostitutes (Tavernier).
Golconda also shared the Mughal **Nauroz**.

136.s: Who began the Mughal custom of jharokha darshan?
136.x: Jharokha darshan was begun by Akbar and ended by Aurangzeb.

136.s: What did Tuladan, adopted by Akbar, involve?
o: Weighing the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday
The emperor appearing daily at a balcony
136.x: Tuladan, a Hindu custom, weighed the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday for gifts to the poor.

136.s: Which Mughal emperor abolished the Nauroz court festival?
136.x: Nauroz, the Persian New Year, was made a court festival by Akbar and abolished by Aurangzeb.

136.s: Nauroz, made a Mughal court festival by Akbar, was the New Year festival of which tradition?
136.x: Nauroz is the Persian New Year; Akbar made it a court festival and Aurangzeb abolished it.

136.s: Tuladan, adopted by Akbar, was originally a custom of which tradition?
136.x: Tuladan, weighing the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday, was a Hindu custom adopted by Akbar.

136.s:
Emperor Akbar is credited with many initiatives to bring about social justice in the society. Which of the following can be considered as his initiatives towards social justice ?

A. Abolition of Jizya.

B. Allowing entry to public offices of the state to all on merit.

C. Discouraging child marriage and encouraging widow remarriage among the Hindus.

D. Restricting the practices of converting prisoners of war to Islam.
136.src: AP Grama Ward Sachivalayam Category-III ANM / Ward Health Se
136.x: All four: Akbar abolished the jizya (1564), opened high office to all on merit (Rajputs and Hindus as mansabdars), discouraged child marriage and allowed widow remarriage, and in 1562 stopped enslaving and forcibly converting prisoners of war.

136.s: Which traveller contrasted the luxury of Mughal nobles with the misery of servants and workmen?
136.x: Pelsaert, the Dutch factor, contrasted nobles' luxury with the misery of servants and workmen.

136.s:
Consider the following statements about slavery in Mughal India:
1. Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war.
2. After Akbar's measure, slaves disappeared from noble households.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
136.x: Akbar stopped enslavement of prisoners of war in 1562, yet noble households remained full of slaves and large domestic staffs.

136.s: Which Mughal emperor stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war?
136.x: Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war in 1562.

136.s: Which measure did Akbar take in 1562?
o: Stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war
136.x: In 1562 Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war. Jizya was abolished in 1564, the pilgrimage tax in 1563, and the Ibadat Khana was built in 1575.
xa: Akbar also tried to stop **forced sati**.
Akbar began **Jharokha darshan** and introduced **sijda / paibos**.
Akbar added **Rajputs** and **Hindustanis** to the nobility.

136.s: In which year did Akbar abolish the jizya?
136.x: Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564, after abolishing the pilgrimage tax in 1563.

136.s: What did Mughal nobles, drawn from Turanis, Iranis, Afghans, Hindustanis, Rajputs and Deccanis, remain dependent on?
136.x: The nobles were wealthy but wholly dependent on the emperor's favour.
xa: ⚠ **Turanis** = Central Asians; **Iranis** = Persians; **Hindustanis** = Indian Muslims.
**Akbar** added **Rajputs** and Hindustanis to balance the Turanis and Iranis.
Under **Aurangzeb**, Deccanis and **Marathas** swelled the nobility; Hindu share about **one-third** (**M. Athar Ali**).

136.s: Which groups dominated the Mughal nobility under Babur and Humayun?
136.x: Turanis and Iranis dominated under Babur and Humayun; Akbar added Rajputs and Hindustanis, and Deccanis and Marathas grew under Aurangzeb.
xa: Hindu share in Aurangzeb's nobility: about **one-third** (**M. Athar Ali**).
**Umara** = top mansabdars, wealthy but dependent on the emperor's favour.
⚠ **Turanis** = Central Asians; **Iranis** = Persians.

136.s: Under Akbar, which groups were added to the Mughal nobility to balance the Turanis and Iranis?
136.x: Akbar added Rajputs and Hindustanis to balance the Turanis and Iranis.

136.s: According to M. Athar Ali, what was the Hindu share of the nobility under Aurangzeb?
136.x: After the Deccan wars Deccanis and Marathas swelled the nobility, and the Hindu share was about one-third.

136.s: Who were referred to as 'Hindustanis' in the Mughal nobility?
136.x: Hindustanis were Indian Muslims; Turanis were Central Asians and Iranis Persians.

136.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Khud-kasht – cultivator of land in another village
Muzarian – tenant cultivating land held by another person
Pahi-kasht – resident peasant cultivating his own village land
Muzarian – resident peasant cultivating his own land
136.x: Muzarian were tenants who cultivated land held by others. Khud-kasht were resident cultivators, while pahi-kasht cultivated land in another village.
xa: ⚠ **Khud** = own village; **Pahi** = another village (non-resident).
Raiyats = **backbone of the economy**; they bore the **land revenue**.
Nobles (**Umara**) were the top **mansabdars**.

136.s: A khud-kasht peasant in Mughal India was one who:
o: Was a tenant of a zamindar
Cultivated land in his own village
136.x: Khud-kasht peasants cultivated land in their own village; pahi-kasht cultivated in another village.

136.s: Who were the 'muzarian' in the Mughal period?
o: Owners of land in their own village
Tenants cultivating land held by others
136.x: Muzarian were tenants who cultivated land held by others, not owners.

136.s: Niccolao Manucci served at the Mughal court first as an artilleryman and later as what?
136.x: Manucci, a Venetian, was an artilleryman and later a physician; he wrote Storia do Mogor.

136.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Peter Mundy – Physician of Dara Shikoh
136.x: Pelsaert, the Dutch factor, wrote Remonstrantie. Bernier was Dara Shikoh's physician, Tavernier the diamond merchant and Mundy an English traveller.

137.s:
Consider the following Mughal structures:
I. Tomb of Salim Chishti
II. Buland Darwaza
III. Tomb of Humayun
IV. Jami Masjid
Which of the above buildings were constructed during the reign of Akbar?
137.x: All four belong to Akbar's reign: the Jama Masjid, Buland Darwaza and Salim Chishti's tomb at Fatehpur Sikri, and Humayun's tomb (1565-72), built by Haji Begum under Akbar.

137.s: Which monument is not at Fatehpur Sikri ?
137.x: Akbari Mahal (Akbar's palace) is in Agra Fort. The Golden Palace (Maryam's palace), Panch Mahal and Jodha Bai's palace are all at Fatehpur Sikri.

137.s: Which of the following was built by Akbar ?
137.x: Akbar built the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri. Akbar also built a Jama Masjid there, but the famous Jama Masjid (Delhi) is Shah Jahan's, the Qutb Minar is Sultanate and the Taj is Shah Jahan's.

137.s: The finest monuments constructed by Akbar are found in–
137.x: Akbar's finest buildings – Buland Darwaza, Jama Masjid, Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas, Jodha Bai's palace – are at Fatehpur Sikri, his capital of 1571-85.

137.s: Which one of the following buildings is known as 'Shani-Fatehpur'?
137.x: The Jama Masjid of Fatehpur Sikri is called 'Shan-i-Fatehpur' (the glory of Fatehpur). The Buland Darwaza is its southern gateway.

137.s: Akbar constructed the 'Buland Darwaza' to commemorate his victory in which region?
137.x: Akbar built the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri to commemorate his conquest of Gujarat (1572-73). Percy Brown linked it to the Deccan victory of 1601, but the standard answer is Gujarat.

137.s: Which monument built by Akbar architected alike Buddhist Monastery ?
137.x: The Panch Mahal at Fatehpur Sikri is a five-storeyed columnar pavilion built in the style of a Buddhist vihara. Diwan-i-Khas, Jodha Bai's palace and the Buland Darwaza are not in this style.

137.s:
Consider the following statements :
Assertion(A) : Constructed ''Buland Darwaza''at Fatehpur Sikri.
Reason(R) : Akbar built this monument to commemorate the birth of his son Jahangir. Which one of the following is correct in reference of above:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are Wrong, but (R) is the correct
137.x: A is true: Akbar built the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri. R is false: it commemorates his victory over Gujarat (1572-73), not the birth of Salim (Jahangir).

137.s:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as
Assertion (A) and the other as
Reason (R).
Assertion (A): Buland Darwaja was constructed at Fatehpur Sikri by the Mughal emperor Akbar.
Reason (R): Akbar built this monument to commemorate the birth of his son Jahangir.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct
137.x: A is true: Akbar built the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri. R is false: it commemorates his victory over Gujarat, not the birth of Jahangir.

137.s: The famous saint Shaikh Salim Chishti lived in-
137.x: Shaikh Salim Chishti lived at Sikri, which Akbar developed into Fatehpur Sikri; Jahangir (Salim) was named after him. Ajmer is the dargah of Muinuddin Chishti.

137.s: In which of the following palace built by Akbar in Fatehpur Sikri the Buddhist architecture was followed?
137.x: The Panch Mahal follows the plan of a Buddhist vihara (five diminishing columnar storeys). Salim Chishti's tomb, the Buland Darwaza and Turkish Sultana's house are not in this style.

137.s: Akbar constructed in Fatehpur Sikri –
137.x: Akbar built the five-storeyed Panch Mahal at Fatehpur Sikri. Moti, Rang and Hira Mahal are not Fatehpur Sikri buildings.

137.s: Which one of the following structures was constructed by Emperor Akbar in Fatehpur Sikri?
137.x: The Panch Mahal is the five-storeyed pillared building at Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri. Moti Mahal, Rang Mahal and Hira Mahal are not Fatehpur Sikri buildings.

137.s:
With respect to the cultural history of India, consider the following statement.

I. White marble was used in making Buland Darwaza and Khankah at Fatehpuri Sikri.

II. Red sandstone and marble were used in making Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow.
Which of the following statements given above is/are correct?
137.x: The Buland Darwaza and Khanqah are red and buff sandstone, and Lucknow's Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza are brick with lime plaster, so neither statement is correct (UPSC official answer d).

137.s: Who built the Panch Mahal at Fatehpur Sikri?
137.x: The Panch Mahal, Buland Darwaza and Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri are Akbar's.
n: Buland Darwaza was constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri was constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Panch Mahal was constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Red Fort at Delhi was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
The monuments at Fatehpur Sikri were constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
xa: **Panch Mahal**: five-storeyed pavilion influenced by **Persian wind towers**.
Akbar also built **Agra Fort**, begun **1565**.
APPSC-G1 **2024**: Salim Chishti's tomb, Buland Darwaza, Humayun's tomb and Jami Masjid all date to Akbar's reign.

137.s: During which period did Fatehpur Sikri serve as Akbar's planned capital?
137.x: Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's capital during 1571-1585 and shows Persian, Indian and Central Asian influences.
xa: Built in honour of **Sheikh Salim Chishti**, mainly in **red sandstone**.
**Jahangir Mahal at Orchha** (MP) continues Akbar's style.
UNESCO World Heritage Site (**1986**).

137.s: Fatehpur Sikri was built in honour of which Sufi saint, after whom Prince Salim was named?
137.x: Fatehpur Sikri was built in honour of Sheikh Salim Chishti, after whom Prince Salim was named.
xs: Fatehpur Sikri was built in honour of **Sheikh Salim Chishti** — option **(2)**.
**Akbar** planned it as his capital, **1571-1585**.
xa: Salim Chishti's white-marble tomb lies in the **Jami Masjid** courtyard.
Main material: **red sandstone**; UNESCO site since **1986**.
Style: blend of **Persian, Indian and Central Asian**.

137.s: Where does Shaikh Salim Chishti's white-marble tomb stand in a Jama Masjid courtyard?
137.x: Salim Chishti's white-marble tomb is in the Jama Masjid courtyard at Fatehpur Sikri.
n: Jahangir's Tomb was built by Jahangir's wife. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Itmad-ud-Daula's Tomb was built from 1622 to 1628. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Shaikh Salim Chishti's Tomb is a famous marble tomb. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Rabia Daurani's Tomb was built in memory of Azam Shah's mother. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
xa: Humayun's Tomb: first **garden tomb**, introduced the **double dome**.
⚠ Some notes name **Hamida Banu Begum** as builder of Humayun's tomb.
"**Taj of the Deccan**" = Bibi ka Maqbara; "**Baby Taj**" = Itimad-ud-Daula.

137.s: Which styles does Jodha Bai's palace at Fatehpur Sikri combine?
o: Hindu trabeate and Islamic arcuate styles
European Gothic and Islamic arcuate styles
137.x: Jodha Bai's palace combines Hindu trabeate construction (beams and lintels) with Islamic arcuate construction (arches and domes).
xa: The **Persian-Indian synthesis**: arch and dome + trabeate, **chhatris**, **Hindu motifs** (Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's tomb).
**Panch Mahal** shows **Persian wind tower** influence.

137.s: For what is the Diwan-i-Khas at Fatehpur Sikri noted?
137.x: The Diwan-i-Khas at Fatehpur Sikri has a single central carved pillar.

137.s: Which arch did Fatehpur Sikri introduce, later used at Jahangir Mahal, Orchha?
137.x: Fatehpur Sikri introduced the Tudor (four-centred) arch, continued at Jahangir Mahal, Orchha.

137.s: Which building at Fatehpur Sikri served as a house of worship where scholars of different religions held philosophical debates?
137.x: The Ibadat Khana was the House of Worship used for philosophical debates among scholars of various religions.
137.tq: Match the building with its precise institutional purpose.
xs: The **Ibadat Khana** was the **House of Worship** for debates among scholars of various religions — option **(2)**.
It was built in **1575** and was part of the religious core of Fatehpur Sikri.
**Jodha Bai's palace** = trabeate + arcuate; **Diwan-i-Khas** = private audience; **Panch Mahal** = five-storeyed pavilion.
xa: The religious core also had the **Jama Masjid** and **Salim Chishti's tomb**.
**Buland Darwaza** was also built c. **1575**.

137.s: Which of the following is NOT at Fatehpur Sikri?
137.x: Akbari Mahal is in Agra Fort, not at Fatehpur Sikri.

137.s: Which event did Akbar commemorate by building the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri?
137.x: The Buland Darwaza (c. 1575) marks Akbar's victory over Gujarat, not Jahangir's birth.

137.s: Which building at Fatehpur Sikri is known as the 'Gate of Magnificence'?
137.x: The Buland Darwaza, the southern entrance to the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri, is called the Gate of Magnificence.

137.s: How many storeys does the Panch Mahal at Fatehpur Sikri have?
137.x: The Panch Mahal is a five-storeyed pillared building; its ground floor has 84 pillars.

137.s: Who built famous Jama Masjid of Delhi ?
137.x: The Jama Masjid of Delhi was built by Shah Jahan (1650-56). Akbar built the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri.

137.s: Who made the Red Fort in Delhi?
137.x: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort (1639-48) as the citadel of his new capital Shahjahanabad, Delhi.

137.s: Who among the following deserves the credit for the construction of ‘Lal Qila’
137.x: The Lal Qila (Red Fort) at Delhi was built by Shah Jahan (1639-48) for Shahjahanabad, not by Akbar, who built the Agra, Lahore and Allahabad forts.

137.s: Which of the following among Mughal Emperors constructed Jama Masjid of Delhi ?
137.x: The Jama Masjid of Delhi was built by Shah Jahan (1650-56).

137.s: Moti Masjid in the Red Fort at Delhi was built by :
137.x: The white-marble Moti Masjid inside the Red Fort, Delhi, was built by Aurangzeb; the Moti Masjid of Agra Fort is Shah Jahan's.

137.s: Jahangir Mahal is located at –
137.x: The Jahangir Mahal built by Akbar for Prince Salim stands inside Agra Fort. (A different Jahangir Mahal is at Orchha, not an option.)

137.s: The mosque, Khair-ul-manzil opposite to the Purana Qila in Delhi was constituted by whom?
137.x: Maham Anga, Akbar's foster-mother, built the Khair-ul-Manazil mosque (1561) opposite the Purana Qila; Hamida Banu was Akbar's mother and Jiji Anga another foster-mother.

137.s: Which among the following mosque has been constructed entirely of marble?
o: Qila-e-Kuhana mosque of Purani Qila in Delhi
137.x: Shah Jahan's Moti Masjid in Agra Fort is entirely of white marble. The Fatehpur Sikri Jama Masjid and the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque are sandstone, and the Delhi Jama Masjid is mainly red sandstone with marble.

137.s: Which of the following forts was not constructed in the reign of Akbar?
137.x: The Red Fort of Delhi was built by Shah Jahan (completed 1648); Agra, Allahabad and Lahore forts are Akbar's.

137.s: The world famous Takht-i-Taus (Peacock Throne) was kept in which of the following Mughal buildings?
o: The Rang Mahal at the Red Fort at Delhi
The Diwan-i-Am at the Red Fort at Delhi
137.x:
Most keys: the Diwan-i-Am, Red Fort (SSC 2006). Strictly: it normally stood in the Diwan-i-Khas of the Red Fort and was moved to the Diwan-i-Am for state occasions (Wikipedia, citing ASI, Bernier, Tavernier).
The Peacock Throne was usually placed in the Diwan-i-Khas of the Red Fort, which is not offered; Tavernier saw it in the Diwan-i-Am, where it was set for state occasions, so the key is the Diwan-i-Am at the Red Fort. It was not in Fatehpur Sikri or the Rang Mahal; Nadir Shah took it in 1739.

137.s: Who built the Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque?
137.x: The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque was built by Sher Shah Suri; Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort and Jama Masjid, Delhi.
n: Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque was constructed by Sher Shah Suri. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Taj Mahal was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Red Fort at Delhi was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Jama Masjid at Delhi was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
xa: Shah Jahan also built the **Moti Masjid** in **Agra Fort**.
⚠ The **Moti Masjid** in the **Red Fort** is **Aurangzeb's**.
The Red Fort's **Diwan-i-Khas** housed the **Peacock Throne**, taken by **Nadir Shah** in **1739**.

137.s: Which of the following statements about the two Mughal structures named Moti Masjid is correct?
o: The Moti Masjid in the Red Fort was built by Aurangzeb, whereas the Moti Masjid in Agra Fort was built by Shah Jahan.
The Red Fort Moti Masjid was built by Shah Jahan, whereas the Agra Fort Moti Masjid was built by Aurangzeb.
Both Moti Masjids were built by Akbar in Agra Fort.
Both Moti Masjids were built by Aurangzeb in Delhi.
137.x: Aurangzeb built the Moti Masjid in the Red Fort, while Shah Jahan built the Moti Masjid in Agra Fort.
137.tq: Resolve the look-alike monument pair by comparing location and builder.
xs: **Red Fort** Moti Masjid = **Aurangzeb**; **Agra Fort** Moti Masjid = **Shah Jahan** — option **(1)**.
Options 2–4 swap or merge the builders; neither Moti Masjid is **Akbar's**.
xa: Shah Jahan also built the **Red Fort** and **Jama Masjid, Delhi**.
Red Fort uses **red sandstone** for structure + **marble** for decoration.

137.s: Who was the architect of Agra Fort?
137.x: Kasim Khan was the architect of Agra Fort, the earliest Akbari-style work.

137.s: Who built the Moti Masjid in Agra Fort?
137.x: The Agra Fort Moti Masjid is Shah Jahan's; Aurangzeb built the one in the Red Fort, Delhi.
xa: Other Fatehpur Sikri buildings: **Buland Darwaza**, **Ibadat Khana**, **Diwan-i-Khas**, Salim Chishti's tomb.
⚠ Moti Masjid: **Red Fort** = Aurangzeb; **Agra Fort** = Shah Jahan.

137.s: In which year did Nadir Shah take the Peacock Throne from the Diwan-i-Khas of the Red Fort?
137.x: Nadir Shah took the Peacock Throne from the Diwan-i-Khas, the private audience hall, in 1739.
xa: The Red Fort's **Moti Masjid** was built by **Aurangzeb**.
**Sheesh Mahal** = mirror-work chambers.

137.s: What was the Rang Mahal in the Red Fort?
o: The palace of the royal women
The hall housing the Peacock Throne
137.x: Rang Mahal was the palace of the royal women; Diwan-i-Am was the hall of public audience.

137.s: In which year did Akbar build Allahabad Fort?
137.x: Akbar built Allahabad Fort in 1583.

137.s: Who rebuilt Lahore Fort?
137.x: Lahore Fort was rebuilt by Akbar; the Red Fort was Shah Jahan's.

137.s: What is the shape of the plan of the Red Fort at Delhi?
137.x: The Red Fort has the shape of an irregular octagon.

137.s: What was the name of the new capital city founded by Shah Jahan at Delhi?
137.x: Shah Jahan built Shahjahanabad, with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid.

137.s: Who built the tomb of Itimal-ud-daula at Agra?
137.x: Nur Jahan built the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula at Agra (1622-28) for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg; Jahangir was the reigning emperor, not the builder.

137.s: Creator of "Bibi Ka Maqbara/ Tomb of Bibi" was –
137.x: Bibi ka Maqbara, the tomb of Aurangzeb's wife Rabia-ud-Daurani at Aurangabad, was built in Aurangzeb's reign by his son Azam Shah, so among the options Aurangzeb is the answer.

137.s: Who among the following has constructed a mausoleum for her emperor husband?
137.x: Haji Begum (Bega Begum), Humayun's widow, built his tomb at Delhi (1565-72); the architects were Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son Sayyid Muhammad.

137.s: Itmad-ud-Daula’s tomb at Agra was built by
137.x: Nur Jahan built Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb at Agra (1622-28) for her father; it is the first Mughal tomb wholly of white marble and the first with pietra dura.

137.s: Who among the following built the tomb of her Emperor husband?
137.x: Haji Begum (Bega Begum), Humayun's widow, built his tomb in Delhi. Mumtaz Mahal and Nur Jahan did not build their husbands' tombs (Nur Jahan built her father's).

137.s: Where is the tomb of Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan situated?
137.x: Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan's tomb is in Delhi (Nizamuddin East, near Humayun's tomb), restored by the Aga Khan Trust and ASI in 2020.

137.s: Which one of the following tombs is called the ‘Second Taj Mahal’:
137.x: Bibi ka Maqbara, the tomb of Rabia-ud-Daurani (Aurangzeb's wife), is called the 'Second Taj' or Taj of the Deccan. Itimad-ud-Daula is the 'Baby Taj'.

137.s: Which historical monument in Delhi is a synthesis of Persian and Indian styles of Architecture?
137.x: Humayun's tomb in Delhi, designed by the Persian Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, is the first synthesis of Persian and Indian styles on a grand scale. The Qutb Minar and Lodi tombs are Sultanate; the Red Fort is later.

137.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

Sher Shah Suri's Tomb was built for himself.

n: Sikandar Lodi's Tomb was built by his son. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Humayun's Tomb was built under the supervision of Haji Begum. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Akbar's Mausoleum was completed by Jahangir. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Sher Shah Suri's Tomb was built for Sher Shah Suri himself. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
xs: The incorrect statement: **Akbar's Mausoleum was completed by Akbar** — option **(3)**.

xa: **Humayun's Tomb** was built from **1565** to **1572**.
Sher Shah's tomb at **Sasaram** was finished under **Islam Shah**.

137.s: At which place is Rabia Daurani's Tomb, also called Bibi ka Maqbara, located?

xs: **Bibi ka Maqbara** is at **Aurangabad** — option **(2)**.

137.s: During which period did Nur Jahan build the marble tomb of her father Itmad-ud-Daula at Agra?

137.s: How was Rabia-ud-Daurani, whose tomb is the Bibi ka Maqbara, related to Aurangzeb?

Rabia Daurani's Tomb was built by Aurangzeb's son, Azam Shah. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]

**Itimad-ud-Daula** = first Mughal tomb in **white marble** with **pietra dura**.

137.s: Which of the following is regarded as the last major imitation in the Mughal garden-tomb tradition?
137.x: Bibi ka Maqbara is regarded as the last major imitation in the Mughal garden-tomb tradition.

137.x: The Taj's white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan. Kishangarh and Rajnagar are later marble centres.

137.s: Who was the chief Architect of Taj Mahal?

137.s: Which of the following Mughal buildings is said to possess the unique feature of being exactly equal in length and breadth?
137.x: The Taj Mahal tomb is equal in length and breadth – a square plan (with chamfered corners) on a square plinth. Forts and the Buland Darwaza have no such plan.

137.s: The design of the Taj Mahal was particularly inspired by which earlier Mughal monument?

137.s: Which one of the following statements about the Taj Mahal is NOT correct?
o: It was built entirely of red sandstone.

UNESCO **1983**; among the **New Seven Wonders** (**2007**).

138.x: Urdu (Hindavi, Rekhta, Lashkari) grew out of military camps and bazaars, mixing Persian, Arabic, Turkic and local speech.

xs: The **Golden Age of Urdu** was the era of **Abdullah Qutb Shah** — option **(2)**.
Court poet **Ghavvasi** wrote the **Tuti Nama** (**1657**) in that era.

Under the Qutb Shahis, **Persian** was official and **Telugu** the people's language.

138.s:
Which of the following statements about visual culture in 18th and early 19th century North India is/are correct?

I. Painters from Patna and Murshidabad flocked to Calcutta and produced water colours in the English mode.

II. Landscape and portraiture became extremely important at this time.

III. The artists Zayan-al-Din. Bhawani Das and Ram Das were adopted by the English East India Company to produce album of India birds and animals.

IV. While Indians were influenced by European artistic styles. Europeans artists did not visit regional courts.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
138.x: I, II and III are true: Patna and Murshidabad painters made English-style watercolours at Calcutta, landscape and portraiture rose, and Zayn-al-Din, Bhawani Das and Ram Das painted birds and animals for the English. IV is false: European artists did visit regional courts.

138.s: ‘Kishan Garh’ School is famous for –
138.x: The Kishangarh school of Rajasthan is famous for painting (Bani Thani).

138.s: The ‘Pahari School,’ ‘Rajput School,’ ‘Mughal School’ and ‘Kangra School’ represent different styles in the art of :
138.x: Pahari, Rajput, Mughal and Kangra are schools of painting.

138.s: With which region was the Pahari school of painting (17th-19th centuries) associated?
138.x: Pahari painting flourished in the Sub-Himalayan region; the Bahmani link belongs to Deccani painting.
xa: Pahari painting grew from painters dispersed after **Aurangzeb** withdrew patronage.
Deccani school: **heavy use of gold**.

138.s: In the court of which dynasty did the Deccani school of painting begin?
138.x: Deccani painting began in the Bahmani court and continued in the successor states of the Bahmani kingdom.
138.tq: Identify the institutional origin of the school.
xs: Deccani painting began in the court of the **Bahmanis** — option **(3)**.
It continued in the **successor states**; at **Golconda** the founder was **Mir Hashim**.
xa: Deccani painting made **heavy use of gold**.
Qutb Shahi Deccani painting was **independent of Mughal style**.

138.s: Under which ruler did the Kangra sub-school of Pahari painting reach its peak?
138.x: Kangra flourished under Raja Sansar Chand.
n: The Pahari School was associated with the north-western Himalayas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
The Rajput School was associated with Rajasthan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
The Kangra School was associated with the Himalayan region. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
The Mughal School was associated with the Mughal Empire. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
xa: Pahari region: **Himachal Pradesh**, **Jammu and Kashmir**, **Tehri Garhwal**, **Paudi Garhwal**.
Rajput style: Hindu epics, **bold colours**, flat 2-D figures.
**Mughal painting influenced** the Pahari, Rajasthani and Kangra schools.

138.s: Who was the major inspiration and patron of the Kishangarh School?
138.x: Raja Sawant Singh (Nagari Das) of Kishangarh was the inspiration and patron of the school. Nihalchand was his painter, while Farrukh Beg and Abul Hasan worked for the Mughals.
138.tq: Discriminate the patron from the painter.
n: Raja Sawant Singh was a major inspiration for the Kishangarh School. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
Raja Sawant Singh was a patron of the Kishangarh School. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
xs: **Raja Sawant Singh** — option **(2)**.
He was the **major inspiration and patron** of the **Kishangarh School**.
**Nihalchand** was the school's artist of **Bani Thani**; **Farrukh Beg** and **Abul Hasan** were Jahangir's painters.
xa: Bani Thani is the Kishangarh school's most famous painting.
Kishangarh artists: **Amirchand**, **Chhotu**, **Bhawanidas**, **Sitaram**.
Abul Hasan was titled **Nadir-uz-Zaman**.

138.s: Who painted the Kishangarh painting 'Bani Thani'?
138.x: Bani Thani is by Nihal Chand, inspired by Sawant Singh's poem Bihari Jas Chandrika.

138.s: Who founded the Deccani school of painting at Golconda?
138.x: Mir Hashim founded Qutb Shahi Deccani painting at Golconda and was later invited to the Mughal court.

139.s: Identify the correct chronology of Later Mughals:
o: Bahadur Shah > Farrukh Siyar > Jahandar Shah > Muhammad Shah > Shah Alam-II

Bahadur Shah Jahandar Shah > Farrukh Siyar > Muhammad Shah > Shah Alam-II
Farrukh Siyar > Jahandar Shah > Muhammad Shah Shah Alam-II > Bahadur Shah
139.x: The order of reigns is Bahadur Shah I (1707-12), Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Farrukhsiyar (1713-19), Muhammad Shah (1719-48) and Shah Alam II (1759-1806). The other options swap Farrukhsiyar and Muhammad Shah or put Bahadur Shah last.

139.s: How did the Mughal Emperor Jahandar Shah's reign come to an early end?
o: He was deposed by his wazir
He died due to a slip while climbing down steps
He was defeated by his nephew in a battle
He died of sickness due to too much consumption of wine
139.x: Jahandar Shah was defeated in 1713 by his nephew Farrukhsiyar, who was backed by the Sayyid brothers, and was then killed. He was not deposed by his own wazir, Zulfiqar Khan.

139.s:
Consider the following statements:
1.
Assertion (A): Shah Alam II spent the initial years as an Emperor far away from his capital.
2.
Reason (R): There was always a lurking danger of foreign invasion from the north‑west frontier. Options:
o: Both A and R are individually true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are individually true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
139.x: Shah Alam II did spend his first years away from Delhi, out of fear of his wazir Imad-ul-Mulk and the court intrigue, living at Allahabad after Buxar. North-western invasions were a real danger, but they were not why he stayed away, so both are true and R does not explain A (UPSC key b).

139.s: The Mughal Emperor at the time of Nadir Shah’s attack was –
139.x: Nadir Shah invaded in 1739 and defeated Muhammad Shah (1719-48) at Karnal. Ahmad Shah, Alamgir II and Rafi-ud-Darajat ruled at other times.

139.s: About Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, it was said that his empire extended from :
139.x:
Most guides: 'Chandni Chowk / Delhi to Palam'. Strictly, the saying 'Sultanat-e-Shah Alam, az Dilli ta Palam' was first made of Shah Alam II, and it was later applied to Zafar.
By Bahadur Shah Zafar's time the emperor's real authority ran only from his Red Fort in Delhi to Palam, which is the 'Chandni Chowk (Lal Qila) to Palam' option. The printed key 'Delhi to Bihar' has no basis, and the printed explanation was about Awadh.

139.s: A group of eunuchs and ladies dominated in the Government under
139.x:
Some guides (and the old app key) give Muhammad Shah. PMF and Spectrum tie the rule of Udham Bai and the eunuch Javed Khan to Ahmad Shah.
Under Ahmad Shah (1748-54) the government was left to the queen mother Udham Bai and her favourite, the eunuch Javed Khan, which is the 'eunuchs and ladies' rule. Muhammad Shah was the pleasure-loving 'Rangeela', but the eunuch-and-harem government belongs to Ahmad Shah's reign.

139.s:
Arrange the following into chronological order and select the correct answer from the codes given below :

139.x: Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Muhammad Shah (1719-48), Ahmad Shah (1748-54) and Alamgir II (1754-59) gives B, A, D, C.

139.s: Which of the following Mughal emperors was not allowed to enter into Delhi by Wazir Ghaziuddin?
139.x: Wazir Ghaziuddin (Imad-ul-Mulk), who had murdered Alamgir II, kept Ali Gauhar (Shah Alam II) out of Delhi. He entered his capital only in 1772 with Maratha help (Mahadji Scindia).

139.s: Who was the last Mughal Emperor to sit on Mayur Singhasan?
139.x: Muhammad Shah was the last Mughal emperor to sit on the Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus), which Nadir Shah carried away in 1739.

139.s: Who succeded Aurangzeb after his death in 1707 AD?
139.x: Aurangzeb was succeeded in 1707 by his son Muazzam as Bahadur Shah I (1707-12). Jahandar Shah, Muhammad Shah and Akbar II came later.

139.s: Which among the following event happened during the reign of Bahadur Shah I?
o: Re-celebration of holi in the imperial court.
139.x: Bahadur Shah I released Shahu, Sambhaji's son, in 1707. Jizya was abolished only after his reign (1713), and he did not revive Holi at court or support sati.

139.s: What was the other name of Roshan Akhtar?
139.x: Roshan Akhtar was the personal name of Muhammad Shah, later nicknamed 'Rangeela'.

139.s: Who among the following Mughal Emperors had the longest reign?
139.x: Muhammad Shah ruled for about 29 years (1719-48), the longest among these. Bahadur Shah I ruled about 5 years, Jahandar Shah 1 and Farrukhsiyar 6.

139.s: At the time, when Nadir Shah attacked Delhi, the Mughal Emperor was
139.x: Nadir Shah attacked in 1739, when Muhammad Shah was emperor, and defeated him at Karnal before sacking Delhi.

139.s: A group of eunuchs and ladies dominated the Mughal court under
139.x: Ahmad Shah (1748-54) left the government to the queen mother Udham Bai and the eunuch Javed Khan, so eunuchs and ladies dominated his court. Muhammad Shah, the tempting option, was the pleasure-loving 'Rangeela', but this coterie rule belongs to Ahmad Shah's reign.

139.s: Who was the Mughal Emperor when the Battle of Plassey was fought between the Nawab of Bengal and the English East India Company?
139.x: Plassey (1757) was fought in the reign of Alamgir II (1754-59). Ahmad Shah's reign ended in 1754 and Shah Alam II's began in 1759.

139.s: Who among the following was responsible for blinding of Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II in 1780?
139.x: The Rohilla Ghulam Qadir blinded Shah Alam II, in 1788 (the stem's 1780 is a misprint). Najib-ud-Daulah was his grandfather, and Mahadji Scindia later punished Ghulam Qadir.

139.s: Bahadur Shah was
o: successor of the Maratha ruler Shivaji.
139.x: Bahadur Shah (Zafar, Bahadur Shah II) was the last Mughal emperor, exiled to Rangoon after 1857. He was not a Lodi, and not a successor of Sher Shah or Shivaji.

139.x: Jahandar Shah (1712-13), Muhammad Shah (1719-48), Ahmad Shah (1748-54) and Alamgir II (1754-59) gives II, I, IV, III.

139.s: The last Mughal Emperor was Bahadur Shah, his father’s name was
139.x: Bahadur Shah Zafar (II) succeeded his father Akbar Shah II (1806-37) in 1837.

139.s: Which Mughal Emperor is known by the name of Rangila?
139.x: Muhammad Shah (1719-48) was called 'Rangeela' for his luxurious, pleasure-loving life. Farrukhsiyar and the two Rafis were the Sayyids' short-lived puppets.

139.s: Which Mughal emperor is known by the name of ‘Rangeela’?
139.x: Muhammad Shah (1719-48) was nicknamed 'Rangeela' for his luxurious life and neglect of administration.

139.s: Which Later Mughal ruler released Shahu?
139.x: Bahadur Shah I, who reigned from 1707 to 1712, released Shahu.
139.tq: Associate the ruler with the specific administrative event.
xs: **Bahadur Shah I** (Muazzam, **1707-1712**) released **Shahu** from Mughal captivity — option **(4)**.
**Farrukhsiyar** was the Sayyids' puppet; **Muhammad Shah** faced Nadir Shah; **Jahandar Shah** was backed by Zulfiqar Khan.
xa: Bahadur Shah I was called "**Shah-i-Bekhabar**".
The **1719** grant gave **chauth and sardeshmukhi** of six Deccan subas to Shahu's agent **Balaji Vishwanath**.

139.s: Ghulam Qadir Rohilla blinded which Mughal emperor in 1788?
139.x: Shah Alam II was blinded by Ghulam Qadir; Ahmad Shah was blinded by Imad-ul-Mulk and Farrukh Siyar by the Sayyids.
xa: **Alamgir II** was murdered by **Imad-ul-Mulk**.
**Bahadur Shah Zafar** was exiled to **Rangoon**, died **1862**.

139.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Farrukhsiyar is correct?
o: He ruled from 1719 to 1748 and faced Nadir Shah's invasion.
He was a puppet of the Sayyid brothers and gave the English duty-free trade in Bengal.
He was the last Mughal emperor and ruled from 1837 to 1857.
He released Shahu immediately after Aurangzeb's death.
139.x: Farrukhsiyar ruled from 1713 to 1719, was controlled by the Sayyid brothers, executed Banda Singh Bahadur in 1716, and granted the English duty-free trade in Bengal.
139.tq: Reject options that attach another Later Mughal's event to Farrukhsiyar.
xs: Farrukhsiyar was a **puppet of the Sayyid brothers** and gave the **English duty-free trade in Bengal** — option **(2)**.
He ruled **1713-1719**; his **1717 farman** is called the Company's "**Magna Carta**".
**1719-1748** and Nadir Shah = **Muhammad Shah**; **1837-1857** = **Bahadur Shah Zafar**; Shahu's release = **Bahadur Shah I**.
xa: He executed **Banda Singh Bahadur** (**1716**).
He was **blinded, deposed and killed** by the Sayyids, **1719**.
He gave Chin Qilich Khan the title **Nizam-ul-Mulk**.

139.s: Which event took place during the reign of Alamgir II?
139.x: The Battle of Plassey (1757) and repeated invasions by Ahmad Shah Abdali occurred during Alamgir II's reign.
xa: Alamgir II (**1754-59**) was **murdered by Imad-ul-Mulk**.
**Third Battle of Panipat**: **14 January 1761**.

139.s: Under whose protection did Shah Alam II return to Delhi in 1771-72?
139.x: After living at Allahabad under Company protection, Shah Alam II returned to Delhi under Mahadji Scindia's protection.
xa: This was in **Madhav Rao I**'s time.
From **1772** **Warren Hastings** stopped his annual grant.

139.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Bahadur Shah II — Exiled to Rangoon after 1857
Shah Alam II — Blinded by Ghulam Qadir Rohilla
Akbar II — Gave Ram Mohan Roy the title ‘Raja’
Muhammad Shah — Exiled to Rangoon after 1857
139.x: Muhammad Shah was not exiled to Rangoon. Bahadur Shah II was exiled to Rangoon after the Revolt of 1857; Shah Alam II was blinded by Ghulam Qadir Rohilla.
139.tq: Find the mismatched ruler and fate by eliminating well-known correct associations.
xs: **Muhammad Shah — exiled to Rangoon** is wrong — option **(4)**.
**Bahadur Shah II (Zafar)** was exiled to **Rangoon** after **1857**.
**Shah Alam II** — blinded by **Ghulam Qadir Rohilla**; **Akbar II** — gave **Ram Mohan Roy** the title "Raja": correct.
xa: Muhammad Shah faced **Nadir Shah** at **Karnal** (**1739**).
Akbar II (**1806-37**) was a **British pensioner**.

139.s: During whose reign were Punjab and Multan ceded to Ahmad Shah Abdali?
139.x: Punjab and Multan were ceded to Ahmad Shah Abdali in the reign of Alamgir II (1754-1759), during Abdali's repeated invasions.

139.s: Which Later Mughal was called 'Lampat' (the profligate)?
139.x: Jahandar Shah, who was under his mistress Lal Kunwar, was called 'Lampat'.

139.s: By what name was Bahadur Shah I called?
139.x: Bahadur Shah I was Shah-i-Bekhabar; Muhammad Shah was Rangeela, Jahandar Shah Lampat and Aurangzeb Zinda Pir.

139.s: Who blinded and deposed the Mughal emperor Ahmad Shah in 1754?
139.x: Imad-ul-Mulk blinded and deposed Ahmad Shah in 1754; Ghulam Qadir blinded Shah Alam II in 1788.

139.s: During whose reign was Banda Singh Bahadur executed in 1716?
139.x: Farrukhsiyar (1713-1719) executed Banda Singh Bahadur in 1716.

139.s: Which Later Mughal is NOT correctly matched with his reign?
139.x: Ahmad Shah ruled 1748-1754, not to 1757, which would overlap Alamgir II.

139.s: Which of the following about the order of accession of the Later Mughals is NOT correct?
o: Bahadur Shah I came before Jahandar Shah
Shah Alam II came before Jahandar Shah
Farrukhsiyar came before Shah Alam II
139.x: The order is Bahadur Shah I, Jahandar Shah, Farrukhsiyar and Shah Alam II, so Shah Alam II came after Jahandar Shah.

139.s: After the revolt of 1857, which Mughal emperor was exiled to Rangoon?
139.x: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar) was exiled to Rangoon and died in 1862; Muhammad Shah was not exiled.

139.s: Who was the wazir of the Mughal emperor Jahandar Shah?
139.x: Jahandar Shah's wazir was Zulfiqar Khan; the Sayyids dominated Farrukhsiyar.

139.s: In which year did the English capture Delhi, during the reign of Shah Alam II?
139.x: The English captured Delhi in 1803, in Shah Alam II's reign.

139.s: Who was the first Mughal pensioner of the East India Company?
139.x: Shah Alam II became the Company's first Mughal pensioner.
xa: **Third Panipat (1761)** and **Buxar (1764)** came in his reign.
**Treaty of Allahabad (1765)**: he granted the **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
Blinded by **Ghulam Qadir Rohilla**, **1788**.

139.s: Who became Mughal emperor immediately after Aurangzeb in 1707?
139.x: Bahadur Shah I (1707-1712) was the first emperor after Aurangzeb, followed by Jahandar Shah.

139.s: Who was the immediate predecessor of Farrukhsiyar on the Mughal throne?
139.x: Farrukhsiyar, with the Sayyid Brothers, killed Jahandar Shah (1712-1713) and took the throne in 1713.

139.x: Bahadur Shah I (1707) came first, then Farrukhsiyar (1713), Muhammad Shah (1719) and Shah Alam II (1759).

139.s: Which Mughal emperor granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the British by the Treaty of Allahabad?
139.x: After Buxar, Shah Alam II gave the Diwani to the Company by the Treaty of Allahabad (1765).

139.s: Where was Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled after the revolt of 1857?
139.x: Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal, was exiled to Rangoon and died there in 1862.

139.s: Who founded the Hyderabad State?
o: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I (Chin Qilich Khan)
139.x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I (Chin Qilich Khan)); it is added as option 5.
Hyderabad State (the Asaf Jahi dominion) was founded by Chin Qilich Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, in 1724, and none of the printed names is he. Quli Qutb Shah founded only Hyderabad city (1591), and Nasir Jung and Muzaffar Jung were later claimants.

139.s: When was Hyderabad State established?
139.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk defeated Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda in 1724 and became virtually independent, so 1724 is Hyderabad State's founding year.

139.s: Give the name of founder of the state of Hyderabad:
139.x: Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded the state of Hyderabad in 1724. Nasir Jung and Muzaffar Jung were his successors and rivals after 1748, and Zulfiqar Khan only envisaged the Deccan state.

139.s: Who among the following was the founder of independent Kingdom of Hyderabad?
139.x: Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded the independent Hyderabad state in 1724 after defeating Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda. Qamaruddin Khan, Muhammad Amin Khan and Asad Khan were other nobles.

139.s: Which year Nizam Ul Mulk Asaf Ja-I died?
139.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, who founded Hyderabad State in 1724, died in 1748.

139.s: Who is the founder of Asaf Jahi dynasty?
139.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020
139.x: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi (Nizam-ul-Mulk, Asaf Jah I) founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724. Nizam Ali Khan, Salabat Jung and Nasir Jung were his sons.

139.s: Who was the last Nizam of the State of Hyderabad?
139.src: Welfare Organiser in AP Sainik Welfare Sub Service 2020
139.x: Mir Osman Ali Khan (1911-48) was the seventh and last Nizam of Hyderabad; Operation Polo ended his rule in 1948. Mir Qamar-ud-din was the first Nizam, and Nizam Ali Khan the second.

139.s: Which dynasty was founded by Nizam-ul-Mulk?
139.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah founded the Asaf Jahi (Asafzahi) dynasty of Hyderabad. The Qutb Shahis were the earlier Golconda dynasty.

139.s: Who was the founder of the Asaf Jahi dynasty in the Deccan?
139.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724. Salar Jung was a 19th-century minister and Nizam Ali the second Nizam.

139.s: Who was the founder of the Asaf Jahi Dynasty in the Deccan?
139.x: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724 after defeating Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda.

139.s: The first Nizam of Hyderabad, who accepted Lord Wellesley's plan of Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, was
139.x: Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II, 1762-1803) accepted Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, the first ruler to do so. Osman Ali Khan was the last Nizam and Nizam-ul-Mulk the first.

139.s: Who was the last Asaf Jahi (Nizam) ruler?
139.x: Mir Osman Ali Khan (1911-48), founder of Osmania University, was the seventh and last Asaf Jahi Nizam. Afzal-ud-Daula and Mahbub Ali Khan came earlier.

139.s:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Hyderabad city? (Select all that apply)
I. Mir Qamar-ud-din Siddiqi was the founder of the Asaf Jahi dynasty and the first Nizam of Hyderabad.
II. The city of Hyderabad, a significant political and economic center in Andhra Pradesh, was established during the rule of Nizam-ul-Mulk in the 18th century.

139.x: Mir Qamar-ud-din Siddiqi (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty and was the first Nizam. Hyderabad city, however, was founded in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, not in Nizam-ul-Mulk's time, so only statement I is correct.

139.s: Asaf Jahi dynasty was founded in which year?
139.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty in 1724; 1748 is the year he died.

139.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk ruled from 1724 until his death in 1748.

139.s: Which of the following is/are not true? (i) Kilich Khan was also known as Mubariz Khan. (ii) Nizam-ul-Mulk defeated Mubariz Khan in Battle of Shakar Kheda. (iii) Julfikar Khan gave Nizam-ul-Mulk with the title of Asaf-Jah.
139.x: Kilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) was not Mubariz Khan; Mubariz was the Mughal governor he defeated at Shakar Kheda (1724), so (ii) is true. The title Asaf Jah came from Muhammad Shah (1725), not Zulfiqar Khan, so (i) and (iii) are untrue.

139.s: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah held which Mughal offices before establishing the Asaf Jahi state?
o: Subedar of the Deccan and Wazir
Nawab of Carnatic and Mir Bakshi
Subedar of Bengal and Diwan of Awadh
Diwan of Bengal and Subedar of Gujarat
139.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk was Subedar of the Deccan and also served as Wazir in the Mughal administration.
139.tq: Distinguish the founder's Mughal offices from those of other successor-state founders.
