168.s: In which year was Kurnool district formed?
168.x: Kurnool was formed in 1858; Anantapur in 1882 and Chittoor in 1911.

168.s: In which year was Anantapur district formed?
168.x: Anantapur district dates from 1882.

168.s: How many collectorates did coastal Andhra have in 1794?
168.x: In 1794 coastal Andhra had five collectorates: Ganjam, Visakhapatnam, Godavari, Krishna and Nellore.

168.s: Which of the following was NOT among the eight collectorates of Andhra by 1856?
168.x: By 1856 the eight collectorates were Ganjam, Visakhapatnam, Godavari, Krishna, Nellore, Bellary, Cuddapah and Kurnool; Anantapur district came only in 1882.

168.s: In 1794, where was the headquarters of the Krishna collectorate?
168.x: Of the five coastal collectorates of 1794, Krishna had its headquarters at Machilipatnam.

168.s: Three East India Company officials were held in great veneration throughout Andhra. The two were Thomas Munro and Arthur Cotton. Who was the third official?
168.x: Sir Thomas Munro is held in high regard in Andhra alongside Sir Arthur Cotton and Charles Phillip Brown, the Telugu scholar who published Vemana; Ripon and Cornwallis were Governors-General, Charles Cotton a distractor.

168.s: Who suppressed the Palegars of Rayalaseema?
168.x: Thomas Munro, Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts from 1800, suppressed the palegars of Rayalaseema; Captain Nolt fought Narasimha Reddy, not the palegars generally.

168.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
168.x: Read and Munro conducted the Baramahal experiment in 1792; Munro's Ceded Districts experiment dates to 1802.
xa: Munro brought **Ryotwari** from the **Bara Mahals** to the Ceded Districts.
Ryotwari extended across **Madras** in **1820** under Governor Munro.
Munro surveyed the Ceded Districts **1802-07**.

168.s: Who became the first Collector of the Ceded Districts in 1800?
168.x: Thomas Munro became the first Collector of the Ceded Districts in 1800, with sub-collectors stationed at Harpanahalli, Kadapa, Adoni and Kurnool.
168.tq: Identify the official associated with the first administrative appointment.
xs: **Sir Thomas Munro** became the **first Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts** in **1800** — option **(1)**.
**Arthur Cotton** was an irrigation engineer; **C.P. Brown** a Telugu scholar; **George Russell** took the Vizianagaram forts after **1794**.
xa: Munro had **four sub-collectors** at **Harpanahalli, Kadapa, Adoni, Kurnool**.
⚠ Some notes say "first Collector … in **1802**" (CDX).
He suppressed the **palegars**, introduced **Ryotwari**, and died at **Pattikonda** on **6 July 1827**.

168.s: Which work is associated with C.P. Brown?
o: The construction of the Krishna anicut
Publication of Vemana’s verses and a Telugu-English dictionary
A survey of the Ceded Districts from 1802 to 1807
Suppression of the palegars of Rayalaseema
168.x: C.P. Brown studied Telugu thoroughly and published Vemana’s verses as well as a Telugu-English dictionary.
168.tq: Match the scholar with his literary contribution.
xs: **C.P. Brown** published **Vemana**'s verses and a **Telugu-English dictionary** — option **(2)**.
The **Krishna anicut** was **Cotton's**; the **1802-07** survey and the suppression of **palegars** were **Munro's**.
xa: Brown studied Telugu thoroughly; with **Munro**, a rare Telugu-learning official.
⚠ **Brown** = Vemana; **Cotton** = anicuts.

168.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Thomas Munro — Introduced Ryotwari and surveyed the districts from 1802 to 1807
C.P. Brown — Built the Dowleswaram anicut
George Russell — Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827
168.x: Munro introduced Ryotwari and surveyed the Ceded Districts during 1802–07. Arthur Cotton was the irrigation engineer, C.P. Brown was the Telugu scholar, and Munro—not George Russell—was Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827.
xs: **Munro** introduced **Ryotwari** and surveyed the districts **1802-07** — option **(1)**.
**Cotton** built the **Dowleswaram anicut**; **Brown** published **Vemana**'s verses; **Munro**, not Russell, was Governor of Madras **1820-27**.
xa: **George Russell** took charge of the Vizianagaram forts after Padmanabham.
⚠ **Cotton**'s assistant = **Veenam Veeranna**; **Brown** = Vemana.

168.s: Which of the following statements about Thomas Munro in the Andhra region is correct?
o: He introduced mahalwari settlement from Punjab into the Ceded Districts and died at Hyderabad in 1827.
He introduced permanent settlement from Bengal into the Circars and died at Madras in 1801.
He introduced zamindari in Rayalaseema and died at Nellore in 1816.
He introduced ryotwari from the Bara Mahals into the Ceded Districts and died at Pattikonda as Governor in 1827.
168.x: Munro brought the ryotwari system from the Bara Mahals to the Ceded Districts. He died at Pattikonda in Kurnool district in 1827 while serving as Governor.
168.tq: Combine the reformer's policy, source region, destination and death details without swapping settlement systems.
xs: **Munro** brought **Ryotwari** from the **Bara Mahals** to the Ceded Districts and died as Governor at **Pattikonda** in **1827** — option **(4)**.
The **Permanent Settlement** was Cornwallis's, not Munro's; Munro died at Pattikonda (**Kurnool**), not Hyderabad.
xa: In Baramahal (**1792**) he worked with **Captain Alexander Read**.
Date of death: **6 July 1827**; Governor of Madras **1820-27**.

168.s: Who suppressed the palegars (poligars) of Rayalaseema and abolished revenue auctions there?
168.x: As Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, Thomas Munro suppressed the palegars and abolished auctions.

168.s: Who executed Sir Arthur Cotton's Krishna anicut at Vijayawada (1855)?
168.x: Cotton designed the Krishna anicut at Vijayawada; it was executed by Captain Charles Orr.

168.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Thomas Munro?
o: He was the first Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts
He introduced Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts in 1802
He was Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827
He depended on dubashis as he did not know Telugu
168.x: Munro was a Telugu-speaking Collector who needed no interpreters; the other statements are correct.

168.s: Which powers did Collectors in the Madras Presidency lose in 1816?
168.x: In 1816 Collectors lost judicial powers; civil justice stayed with the District Judge.

168.s: Which of the following are present-day silk hubs of Rayalaseema?
168.x: Dharmavaram and Madanapalle are present-day silk hubs; sericulture was promoted by the British in the Ceded Districts in the late 19th-early 20th centuries.
xa: Ceded Districts = **Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur, Bellary**.
Name **Rayalaseema** adopted in **1928**.

168.s: The growing gap between the fertile, educated Circars and the dry, neglected Ceded Districts later influenced the debate on which pact?
168.x: The contrasting development of the Circars and the Ceded Districts later shaped the Sri Bagh Pact debate. The other pacts belong to different political contexts.
168.tq: Link a regional socio-economic contrast with the agreement it later influenced.
xs: The divergence between the **fertile, educated Circars** and the **arid, neglected Ceded Districts** later shaped the **Sri Bagh Pact** debate — option **(2)**.
The Circars came to the Company in **1766**; the Ceded Districts only in **1800**, and they grew apart under British rule.
xa: Ceded Districts = today's **Rayalaseema**; name adopted at **Nandyal, 1928**.
The Circars correspond to **Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, East and West Godavari, Krishna + Guntur**.

168.s: By which of the following was the post of District Judge, under whom the Zilla Court functioned, created?
168.x: The post of District Judge was created under the Cornwallis Code of 1793. The Madras Regulations of 1816 related chiefly to Munsiff and Panchayat courts.
168.tq: Use the legislation–office association and reject neighbouring judicial enactments.
xs: The **District Judge** post was created by the **Cornwallis Code, 1793** — option **(1)**.
The **Madras District Police Act** came in **1859**; the **Madras Regulations of 1816** set up **Munsiff** and **Panchayat** courts.
xa: District courts were also called **Zilla** courts.
After the **1816** separation, civil justice stayed with the District Judge.

168.s: The introduction of British judicial procedure in place of village panchayats was criticised mainly because it:
o: was slow and costly and contributed to litigation and debt
made justice quicker and less expensive
reduced litigation and eliminated rural debt
transferred all judicial powers to hereditary village officers
168.x: British judicial procedure displaced village panchayats and was criticised as slow and costly. It increased litigation and contributed to indebtedness.
168.tq: Select the option that combines all the stated consequences without reversing the criticism.
xs: British procedure was **slow and costly** and fed **litigation and debt**, displacing village panchayats — option **(1)**.
It did not make justice quicker or cheaper, nor reduce rural debt.
xa: **Munro**'s **1816** Regulations set up **Munsiff** and **Panchayat** courts as courts of first instance.
Village officials handled **petty thefts**.
The **District Collector** became the pivot of British rule and ended village autonomy.

168.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the judicial hierarchy in the Madras Presidency?
168.x: The Munsiff Court functioned at the taluk level, while the Zilla Court functioned at the district level. Sadar Adalats were apex courts for natives at Madras.
168.tq: Use the administrative level as the anchor for matching the court.
xs: **Taluk — Munsiff Court** is correct — option **(3)**.
The **Zilla Court** was at the **district** level; **Sadar Adalat** was the apex civil court at Madras.
xa: Appeal: **Provincial Courts of Appeal / Circuit courts** (powers expanded in **1820**).
Apex criminal court: **Sadar Faujdari Adalat**.
**Madras Supreme Court (1801)** for British subjects in Madras town.

168.s: In which year was the Indian Penal Code enacted?
168.x: The IPC dates to 1860; the CPC to 1859 and the CrPC to 1861.
xa: **Madras District Police Act** — also **1859**.
Criticism: slow, costly British procedure displaced village **panchayats** → litigation and debt.

168.s: In which year was the Judicial Commission, with Thomas Munro as President, constituted?
168.x: Munro presided over the Judicial Commission of 1814; its report was submitted in April 1816 and largely accepted.
xa: Result: the **Madras Regulations of 1816** — Munsiff and Panchayat courts.
**1818**: magistrates got powers to punish.

168.s: What did the Madras Regulations of 1816 provide for?
o: Abolition of all village-level judicial institutions
Munsiff and Panchayat courts as courts of first instance
Transfer of civil justice from District Judges to Collectors
Creation of the Madras High Court
168.x: The Madras Regulations of 1816 established Munsiff courts and Panchayat courts in every large village and district as courts of first instance.
168.tq: Match the regulation with its immediate institutional reform.
xs: The **Madras Regulations of 1816** set up **Munsiff and Panchayat courts** as **courts of first instance** — option **(2)**.
They strengthened, not abolished, village-level justice: village officials handled **petty thefts**.
xa: Panchayat courts were set up in every large village and district.
Same year (**1816**): Collectors lost judicial powers; civil justice stayed with **District Judges**.
Munro (**1816**) moved **police supervision** from judges to **Collectors**.

168.s: Who created thanas under the supervision of darogas in the early British police administration?
168.x: Cornwallis created thanas under darogas, who were Indian officers assisted by constables. Darogas were criticised for abusing their power.
168.tq: Use the founder–institution association and avoid swapping judicial and police reformers.
xs: **Lord Cornwallis** created **thanas** under **darogas** (Indian officers) with constables — option **(4)**.
Darogas were known for **abuse of power**.
xa: In **Madras**, village watchmen were supplemented by central police under a **District Superintendent**.
**Munro (1816)** moved police supervision from judges to **Collectors**.
**Madras District Police Act**: **1859**.

168.s: Munro's police reforms of 1816 transferred police supervision from:
o: Darogas to the Board of Revenue
168.x: Munro's changes in 1816 transferred police supervision from judges to Collectors. This was part of the reorganisation of administrative powers.
168.tq: Test the direction of transfer by identifying both the former and new authority.
xs: **Munro**'s **1816** reform moved police supervision **from judges to Collectors** — option **(1)**.
**Darogas** belonged to **Cornwallis'** thana system; the **District Superintendent** headed the central police.
xa: Munro presided over the **Judicial Commission (1814)**; report **April 1816**.
Under ryotwari, some magisterial powers returned to Collectors.
The Collector combined **revenue + magisterial + police** powers — the pivot of British rule.

168.s: Which was the court at the taluk level under Company rule?
168.x: The Munsiff court sat at the taluk level, below the Zilla court.

168.s:
Consider the following statements about the courts of the Madras Presidency:

168.x: The Sadar Faujdari Adalat was the apex criminal court and the Madras Supreme Court dates from 1801; the Zilla court was under a District Judge.

168.s: In which year was the Madras District Police Act passed?
168.x: The Madras District Police Act was passed in 1859.

168.s: When did Munro submit his report as President of the Judicial Commission?
168.x: The Judicial Commission (1814) under Munro reported in April 1816 and its report was mostly accepted.

168.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the May 2026 Supreme Court plea for a separate revenue judicial service cadre?
o: It argued that revenue officers lack legal training to decide land-title disputes
It invoked Article 368 of the Constitution
The Supreme Court issued notice on the plea
It invoked Article 14 of the Constitution

169.s: In which year was the Dowleswaram dam constructed on the Godavari river?
169.x: The Dowleswaram (Godavari) anicut was begun in 1847 and completed in April 1852 (NextGen L3 p.49 says 1849); the Krishna anicut followed in 1855.

169.s: Who was the Andhra official who helped Sir Arthur Cotton in the construction of the Godavari dam?
169.x: Veenam Veeranna was the Indian official who assisted Arthur Cotton at Dowleswaram; he was made Rao Bahadur and Assistant Engineer.

169.s: Who among the following was the English officer who assisted Sir Arthur Cotton in the construction of the Krishna barrage and the Dowleswaram dam?
169.x: Captain (Charles) Orr executed the Krishna anicut on Cotton's plan; Captain Nolt fought Narasimha Reddy, and the others are distractors.

169.s: Who said that the project named Ramapada Sagaram near Polavaram will be built?
169.x: The Ramapada Sagar reservoir near Polavaram was the dream-child of (Sonti) S.V. Ramamurthi, ICS, who named it after the backwaters reaching Lord Rama's feet at Bhadrachalam; Cotton built Dowleswaram and K.L. Rao was a later minister.

169.s: Who is regarded as the Pioneer of Irrigation works in South India?
169.x: Sir Arthur Cotton, builder of the Godavari and Krishna anicuts, is regarded as the pioneer of irrigation in South India; Baird Smith worked on the Ganga canal.

169.s: Due to whose efforts an anicut across the Godavari river at Dowaleshwaram was completed in 1849?
169.x: The Godavari anicut at Dowleswaram (1847-52) was designed and built by Sir Arthur Cotton; Munro, Macpherson and Barlow were governors. (Moved to the Andhra-under-the-Company row.)

169.s:
A: Even though the British East India Company occupied the region, during their rule they focused extensively on irrigation infrastructure to boost agricultural productivity.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

169.x: A is false: the Company's rule was revenue-driven and irrigation was neglected for long; R is true: Arthur Cotton's anicuts on the Godavari (Dowleswaram, from 1847) and the Krishna (from 1852-53) were the major exceptions.

169.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Veenam Veeranna — Andhra assistant to Arthur Cotton
169.x: The Dowleswaram anicut was built across the Godavari. Arthur Cotton built the Krishna anicut at Vijayawada, and Veenam Veeranna served as his Andhra assistant.

**Veenam Veeranna** = **APPSC G2 2019** key.

169.s: By what name are the Godavari and Krishna deltas together known in Andhra?
169.x: The Godavari and Krishna deltas are called the Rice Bowl of Andhra because of their importance for rice cultivation.
xa: **Rice** was the main crop under British rule.
The Cotton Barrage irrigates **10 lakh acres**.

169.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Dowleswaram anicut?
o: Arthur Cotton reported to the Board of Revenue on it in 1844.
Its Indian assistant Veenam Veeranna was made Rao Bahadur and Assistant Engineer.
Work on it began in 1847 and its main work was completed in April 1852.

169.s: Across which river is the Sangam anicut, which supplies Nellore's canals, built?
169.x: The Sangam anicut (1882–86) is on the Penna in Nellore.

169.s: Who originally proposed the Krishna anicut at Bezwada?
169.x: It was proposed by Col. Henry Atlock (Lake) and built by Captain Charles Orr on Cotton's plan.

169.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
169.x: The Bezwada anicut (Prakasam Barrage) is on the Krishna; Dowleswaram is on the Godavari and Sangam on the Penna.

169.s: Automated crest-gate telemetry and SCADA were installed at which barrage in February 2026?
169.x: Automated crest-gate telemetry and SCADA were installed at the Prakasam Barrage in February 2026.
169.tq: Apply the location-and-year pair to distinguish similar irrigation structures.
xs: Telemetry and **SCADA** were installed at the **Prakasam Barrage** in **Feb 2026** — option **(3)**.
The Prakasam Barrage stands on the old **Krishna anicut** at **Bezwada**.
xa: The **Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage** (Godavari) is getting **117** new gates.

169.s: Who proposed the Ramapada Sagaram project, the forerunner of today's Polavaram project?
169.x: Ramapada Sagaram, the forerunner of Polavaram, was proposed by Sir Shonthi Venkataramamurthy.

169.x: Work on Dowleswaram began in 1847 and the main work was completed in April 1852; 1855 is the Krishna anicut.

169.s: By what name is the Krishna anicut at Bezwada known today?
169.x: The Krishna anicut at Bezwada (Vijayawada), completed in 1855, is now the Prakasam Barrage.

169.s:
Consider the following statements about Sir Arthur Cotton:
1. He was knighted in 1861.
2. He was popularly called "Apara Bhagiratha" and "Cotton Dora".
3. On his suggestion, Rajahmundry and Machilipatnam districts were renamed Krishna and Godavari respectively.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
169.x: Statement 1 is correct: Cotton was knighted in 1861. Statement 2 is correct: he was called Apara Bhagiratha and Cotton Dora. Statement 3 is wrong: Rajahmundry became Godavari and Machilipatnam became Krishna, not the reverse. So 1 and 2 only; '1 only' misses statement 2, and the options with 3 are wrong.
169.tq: Rajahmundry sits on the Godavari, so it became Godavari district.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: Cotton was **knighted in 1861**.
Statement 2: he was called "**Apara Bhagiratha**" and "**Cotton Dora**".
Statement 3 wrong: in **1859** Rajahmundry became **Godavari** and Machilipatnam **Krishna** — the statement swaps them.
xa: Cotton's **1844** report urged an anicut near **Rajahmundry**.
His assistant: **Veenam Veeranna** at **Dowleswaram**.

169.s: Who among the following was made 'Rao Bahadur' for helping Sir Arthur Cotton build the Dowleswaram anicut?
169.x: Veenam Veeranna was Cotton's Indian officer at Dowleswaram and was made Rao Bahadur and Assistant Engineer.

169.s: What was the immediate trigger for Arthur Cotton's proposal for an anicut near Rajahmundry?
169.x: The Guntur famine of 1832–33 prompted the proposal for an anicut near Rajahmundry.
169.tq: Link a public-works proposal with its immediate historical cause.
xs: The trigger was the **Guntur famine (1832-33)** — option **(2)**.
Cotton's report followed in **1844**, leading to the **Dowleswaram** anicut.
xa: The **Buckingham Canal** was extended as famine relief in **1876-78**.
Reduced land under food crops made the region **famine-prone**.

169.s: What is the name of the Rajahmundry Sub-Collector who started Anglo-Vernacular schools in most parts of Andhra?

169.s: What is the name of the Rajahmundry Sub-Collector who started schools in Anglo-Vernacular languages in most parts of Andhra?
169.x: G.N. Taylor, Sub-Collector of Rajahmundry, opened Anglo-vernacular schools at several places in Andhra; Rev. Noble founded the Machilipatnam school.

169.s: Name the Sub-Collector of Rajahmundry who opened Anglo-vernacular schools at several places in Andhra
169.x: G.N. Taylor, Sub-Collector of Rajahmundry, opened Anglo-vernacular schools at several places in Andhra; Rev. Noble founded the Machilipatnam school.

169.s: Three English officers are revered in Andhra region, two of them are Thomas Munro and Arthur Cotton and the third person is?
169.x: Sir Thomas Munro is held in high regard in Andhra alongside Sir Arthur Cotton and Charles Phillip Brown, the Telugu scholar who published Vemana; Ripon and Cornwallis were Governors-General, Charles Cotton a distractor.

169.s: In which area did Mr. Taylor start a private school?
169.x: George Noble Taylor founded a school at Narsapur in 1852 (later the Taylor High School); Machilipatnam's school was Rev. Noble's.

169.s: Which of the following was associated with C.P. Brown?
o: Serving as the first Surveyor General in 1815
Introducing ryotwari and suppressing the palegars
Editing the Madras Literary Journal and serving as Curator of the Madras Manuscript Library
169.x: C.P. Brown contributed to Telugu revival, edited the Madras Literary Journal and served as Curator of the Madras Manuscript Library.

o: Awadh — 1856 — annexation due to absence of a natural heir

**Punjab (1849)** was a **conquest** after the **Second Anglo-Sikh War**, not lapse.
**Berar (1853)** was taken from the Nizam for **arrears**.

**Sindh (1843)** came before Dalhousie — a conquest under **Ellenborough**.

B. Satara
C. Jhansi

xs: **Satara, Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Jhansi** were all taken by **lapse** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Punjab** and **Lower Burma** were taken by **conquest**, and **Berar** from the Nizam for **arrears** — option 1 fails.
**Awadh** was annexed for **misgovernment**; for **Tanjore** and the **Carnatic** only titles and pensions were abolished — option 2 fails.
**Sindh (1843)** and **Punjab (1849)** were **conquests** — option 4 fails.
xa: Lapse dates: **Satara 1848**, **Jaitpur 1849**, **Sambalpur 1849**, **Baghat 1850**, **Udaipur 1852**, **Jhansi 1853**, **Nagpur 1854**.
**UPPSC 2025** key: **Karnataka (Carnatic)** was not a lapse case.

170.s: Which of the following states was annexed on the ground of maladministration, rather than under the Doctrine of Lapse?

170.tq: Find the exception by separating policy-based annexations from administrative grounds.
xs: **Awadh** was annexed in **1856** for **maladministration** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The ground rested on reports by Residents **Sleeman** and **Outram**; the ruler dispossessed was **Wajid Ali Shah**.
**Sambalpur (1849)**, **Jhansi (1853)** and **Nagpur (1854)** were all **lapse** annexations.
xa: Other non-lapse cases: **Punjab** and **Lower Burma** by conquest; titles and pensions abolished for **Tanjore** and the **Carnatic**.
The Awadh takeover turned **taluqdars** and sepoys against the Company before **1857**.
Earlier, Awadh was Warren Hastings' classic **buffer** state, shielding Bengal.

170.s: Whom did the lapse annexations and the takeover of Awadh alienate, helping to cause the Revolt of 1857?
170.x: The annexations and Awadh takeover turned rulers, taluqdars and sepoys against the Company, contributing to the revolt.
170.tq: Connect a political policy with its stated social and military reaction.
xs: The **lapse** annexations and the **Awadh** takeover turned **rulers, taluqdars and sepoys** against the Company — so option **(2)** is correct.
As a result the policy was **abandoned after 1857**.
xa: After **1858**, annexation stopped and the **right of adoption** was recognised (subordinate union).
**Awadh (1856)** was annexed for **misgovernment**; its Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was dispossessed.
At **Hyderabad** in **1857**, **Turrebaz Khan** attacked the Residency on **17 July** to free **Chida Khan**; repulsed by **Davidson**.

o: the Sikh army crossing the Sutlej
the murder of British officers Vans Agnew and Anderson at Multan
the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh
the sale of Kashmir to Gulab Singh

181.s: Who was the adoptive father of Nana Saheb, whose pension was denied to him?
181.x: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa, whose pension was stopped.

181.s: With which of the following was Begum Hazrat Mahal's political grievance during the Revolt of 1857 mainly connected?
o: the loss of the Red Fort by Mughal successors
the annexation of Awadh and the proclamation of her son Birjis Qadr as ruler
the confiscation of Kunwar Singh’s estates
the denial of Baji Rao II’s pension
181.x: Begum Hazrat Mahal opposed the annexation of Awadh and had her son Birjis Qadr proclaimed ruler.
181.tq: Match the leader with the specific grievance and associated claimant.
xs: **Begum Hazrat Mahal** (Lucknow) resented the **annexation of Awadh**; her son **Birjis Qadr** was proclaimed ruler — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Red Fort** grievance was **Bahadur Shah Zafar's**; the **pension** grievance **Nana Saheb's**.
xa: ⚠ **Kanpur** = Nana Saheb; **Lucknow** = Begum Hazrat Mahal; **Jagdishpur** = Kunwar Singh; **Bareilly** = Khan Bahadur Khan.
Awadh's Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was exiled to Calcutta.

181.s: Which of the following grievances was associated with Nana Saheb?
o: Denial of the pension of his adoptive father, Baji Rao II
Refusal to recognise his adopted son as ruler of Jhansi
Removal from the Red Fort and loss of the imperial title
181.x: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, was denied the pension of his adoptive father.
181.tq: Match the leader with his personal political grievance, avoiding swapped revolutionary leaders.
xs: **Nana Saheb** was denied the pension of his adoptive father **Baji Rao II** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jhansi** throne = **Rani Lakshmibai**; **Jagdishpur** estates = **Kunwar Singh**; Red Fort/title = **Bahadur Shah Zafar**.
xa: Baji Rao II was the **last Peshwa**.
Nana Saheb led the revolt at **Kanpur**.

181.s: The Revolt of 1857 began at which place?
181.x: The Revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on 10 May 1857, when sepoys rose and marched to Delhi.
181.tq: Recall where the 1857 revolt broke out.
n: Meerut was associated with the beginning of the Revolt of 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
xs: The Revolt of **1857** began at **Meerut** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Delhi** (Bahadur Shah II), **Kanpur** (Nana Sahib) and **Lucknow** (Begum Hazrat Mahal) were later centres of the revolt.
xa: Delhi's leader faced British opponent **John Nicholson**.
**Rani Lakshmibai** of **Jhansi** was opposed by **Hugh Rose**.
Important leaders: **Bahadur Shah II**, **Rani Lakshmibai**, **Nana Sahib**, **Kunwar Singh**.

181.s: Which of the following pairs (centre of 1857 – leader) is correctly matched?
181.x: Begum Hazrat Mahal led at Lucknow; Bahadur Shah II led at Delhi, Nana Sahib at Kanpur and Kunwar Singh at Jagdishpur.
n: Bahadur Shah II was associated with Delhi during 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Kanpur was associated with Nana Sahib during 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Lucknow was associated with Begum Hazrat Mahal during 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Jhansi was associated with Rani Lakshmibai during 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Jagdishpur was associated with Kunwar Singh during 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
xa: **Tatya Tope** was the **commander** at Kanpur; **Khan Bahadur Khan** led at **Bareilly**.
**Faizabad** — **Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah**; **Assam** — **Maniram Dutt**.
⚠ Nana Saheb's grievance: the pension of his adoptive father **Baji Rao II** was stopped.

181.s: Who led the assault that recaptured Delhi from the rebels in 1857?
181.x: John Nicholson led the assault on Delhi; Hugh Rose took Jhansi, Colin Campbell relieved and recaptured Lucknow, and Henry Lawrence died defending the Lucknow Residency.
n: John Nicholson was associated with Delhi during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Hugh Rose was associated with Jhansi and Rani Lakshmibai during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Colin Campbell was associated with Lucknow during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Henry Lawrence was associated with Lucknow during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
xa: Other British names at Lucknow: **Havelock** and **Neil**.
Lucknow's rebel leader was **Begum Hazrat Mahal**, who proclaimed her son **Birjis Qadr** ruler.
Jhansi had **lapsed** in **1853** when the Rani's adopted son was denied the throne.

181.s: Who led the Revolt of 1857 at Bareilly?
181.x: Khan Bahadur Khan led at Bareilly; Kunwar Singh led at Jagdishpur in Bihar, Ahmadullah Shah at Faizabad and Tatya Tope in Central India.
n: The 1857 Revolt was centred at Bareilly under Khan Bahadur Khan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Khan Bahadur Khan was the leader at Bareilly during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
The 1857 Revolt was centred at Bihar and Jagdishpur under Kunwar Singh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Kunwar Singh was the leader at Bihar and Jagdishpur during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
The 1857 Revolt was centred at Faizabad under Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah was the leader at Faizabad during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
The 1857 Revolt was centred in Central India under Tatya Tope. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Tatya Tope was the leader in Central India during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
xa: **Assam** — **Maniram Dutt**.
Khan Bahadur Khan was a **Rohilla** chief.
**Delhi** — **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, opposed by **John Nicholson**.

181.s: Begum Hazrat Mahal proclaimed which of her sons as ruler of Awadh in 1857?
181.x: Begum Hazrat Mahal declared her son Birjis Qadr ruler at Lucknow.
181.tq: one-liner

181.s: Where did Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah, who led the revolt at Faizabad, originally come from?
181.x: Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah, the bitterest enemy of the British, came from Chinapattan (Madras).
181.tq: one-liner

181.s: Which of the following pairs (centre – British opponent) is correctly matched?
181.x: Colin Campbell retook Lucknow in 1858; Henry Lawrence died defending the Residency.

181.s: Where did Thakur Kushal Singh lead the Revolt of 1857?
181.x: Thakur Kushal Singh led the revolt at Auwa (Rajputana) and beat the British-Jodhpur army.

181.s: Who led the Revolt of 1857 in Assam?
181.x: Maniram Dutt (Dewan) led the revolt in Assam.

181.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Jagdishpur was located in Bihar.
2. Khan Bahadur Khan led the Revolt of 1857 at Bareilly.
3. Khan Bahadur Khan led the Revolt of 1857 at Jagdishpur.
Which of the above statements are correct?
181.x: 1 and 2 are correct; 3 is wrong because Jagdishpur was led by Kunwar Singh.
n: Jagdishpur was located in Bihar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Bareilly was associated with Khan Bahadur Khan during 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
xa: Kunwar Singh was a zamindar ruined by loss of his estates.
**Faizabad** — **Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah**.
⚠ **Kanpur** = Nana Saheb; **Lucknow** = Begum Hazrat Mahal; **Jagdishpur** = Kunwar Singh; **Bareilly** = Khan Bahadur Khan.

181.s: Rani Lakshmibai's grievance under the Doctrine of Lapse was that:
o: Her adopted son was refused the throne
181.x: Under the Doctrine of Lapse Jhansi was annexed and Lakshmibai's adopted son was refused the throne.
181.tq: one-liner

181.s: Which one of the following was NOT a condition of the Subsidiary Alliance devised by Lord Wellesley?
o: The ruler had to maintain a British subsidiary force at his own cost
The ruler had to accept a British Resident
The ruler had to exclude other Europeans from his service
The ruler could freely conduct an independent foreign policy
181.x: A subsidiary ally had to surrender independent foreign-policy control. The other conditions were part of the system devised by Wellesley.
181.tq: Spot the option that reverses the central consequence of the alliance.
xs: A subsidiary ally could **not** run an **independent foreign policy** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Real terms: keep a **British subsidiary force** at his cost, accept a **British Resident**, no other **Europeans** in service.
xa: The ruler also had to **disband his own army**; unpaid subsidy → **ceding territory**.
Devised by **Lord Wellesley, 1798**.
First to accept: **Nizam of Hyderabad** (**September 1798**).

181.s: By what name did the Rayalaseema districts ceded by the Nizam under the 1800 treaty come to be known?
181.x: The Nizam ceded the Rayalaseema districts in 1800 to meet the cost of the subsidiary force; these became known as the Ceded Districts.
181.tq: Link the treaty, territorial transfer and historical regional name.
xs: The Rayalaseema districts ceded in **1800** became the **"Ceded Districts"** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They paid for the **subsidiary force** kept for the Nizam.
xa: The Nizam was the **first** subsidiary ally (**September 1798**), again **1800**.
AP angle: asked in **APPSC G2 2002, 2008**.

181.s: Who was the first Indian ruler to accept Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance in September 1798?
181.x: The Nizam of Hyderabad was first, in September 1798 (and again in 1800). Mysore followed in 1799, Awadh in November 1801, and the Peshwa signed through the Treaty of Bassein.
181.tq: First subsidiary ally = Nizam, 1798.
xs: The **Nizam of Hyderabad** was first, in **September 1798** (again **1800**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Mysore** followed in **1799**, **Awadh** in **November 1801**, the **Peshwa** in **December 1802** (Treaty of Bassein).
xa: AP angle: asked in **APPSC G2 2002, 2008**.
The **1800** treaty created the **"Ceded Districts"** (Rayalaseema).

181.s: When did the Peshwa accept the Subsidiary Alliance through the Treaty of Bassein?
181.x: The Peshwa accepted it in December 1802 by the Treaty of Bassein; Awadh had accepted in November 1801, Bhonsle in December 1803 and Scindia in February 1804.

181.s: Which was the last Maratha power to accept the Subsidiary Alliance (1818)?
181.x: Holkar, in 1818, was the last Maratha power to sign; Bhonsle signed in 1803 and Scindia in 1804.
181.tq: one-liner

181.s: Which states accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1799?
181.x: Mysore and Tanjore came under the Subsidiary Alliance in 1799.

182.s:
Consider the following statements with reference to the ‘Revolt of 1857’ :
1. Syed Ahmad Khan wrote “Causes of the Indian Revolt”.
2. Mangal Pande was hanged on March 29, 1857.
3. Hazrat Mahal led the revolt at Lucknow.
4. Nana Saheb led the revolt at Bareilly.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
182.x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (Only 1 & 3); it is added as option 5.
1 is true (Syed Ahmad Khan wrote Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind, 'The Causes of the Indian Revolt') and 3 is true (Hazrat Mahal led at Lucknow). 2 is false: Mangal Pandey's attack was on 29 March 1857 but he was hanged on 8 April 1857; 4 is false: Nana Saheb led at Kanpur, Bareilly was Khan Bahadur Khan. No printed code gives 1 and 3 only (printed key 2, 3 & 4 is wrong).

182.s:
Which of the following was/were the impact on sepoys that causes the revolt among sepoys?

a. Indian sepoys despite their valour and great fighting capacity, never rose to the rank of Subedar.

b. Beef and pig fat greased cartridges were to be used in new Enfield rifle.

c. The maintenance amount spent on Indian sepoys were only half of their British counterparts.
182.src: AP recruitment paper (header page missing in scan)
182.x: a (no Indian could rise above Subedar) and b (Enfield cartridges greased with beef and pig fat) are the grievances the sources state; c's 'half' figure is not supported – the sources only say the sepoy was paid much less.

182.s: On which date, 1857 mutiny had been started in Meerut?
182.src: APPSC Extension Officer Grade-I Common Paper General Studies
182.x: The Meerut rising began on 10 May 1857.

182.s: Which rifle had a greased catridge made of cow or pig fat causing revolt amongst sepoys of British Army in India?
182.x: The Enfield rifle's greased cartridges (cow and pig fat) triggered the revolt.

182.s: The symbol of 1857 independence struggle was –
182.x: Lotus and chapatis were the symbols of the 1857 struggle.

182.s: When was the new Enfield Rifle with greased cartridges introduced in the British Indian Army?
182.x: The Company decided to replace the Brown Bess with the Enfield rifle in December 1856, with training at Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot; accounts vary (late 1856 to January 1857), and December 1856 is the date the notes and key give.

182.s: The immediate cause of India’s First War of Independence was
o: Doctrine of Lapse by Lord Dalhousie.
Suspicion about British interference in religion.
182.x: The greased cartridges made sepoys suspect British interference in their religion – the immediate cause; lapse, military discontent and economic exploitation were long-term causes.

182.s: The immediate cause of India's first war of independence in 1857 was
182.src: APPSC Junior Assistant cum Computer Assistant in ANGRAU Gene
182.x: The new Enfield rifle with its greased cartridges was the immediate cause.

182.s: Across which region were mysterious chapatis passed from village to village before the Revolt of 1857?
182.x: The chapatis passed village to village across North India, not South India.
xa: The **Enfield** cartridges were believed greased with **cow and pig fat**.
All read as a plot to **force conversion**.

182.s: Who is regarded as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857?
182.x: Mangal Pandey is identified as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857.
182.tq: Test a first-in-sequence fact directly, while using other prominent figures as nearby distractors.
xs: **Mangal Pandey** is the **first martyr of 1857** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He attacked **Lt Baugh** and **Sergeant-Major Hewson** at **Barrackpore** on **29 March 1857**.
xa: He was hanged on **8 April 1857**; his regiment (**34th Bengal NI**) was disbanded.
On **21 July 2026** the PM paid tribute on his birth anniversary (born **19 July 1827**).
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** on **11-12 May 1857**.

182.s: Why did the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle offend both Hindu and Muslim sepoys?
o: They were believed to contain cow and pig fat, and had to be bitten open.
They required sepoys to cross the sea before use.
They were made exclusively from animal skin.
They were distributed only to European soldiers.
182.x: The greased-paper cartridges were believed to contain cow fat, offensive to Hindus, and pig fat, offensive to Muslims. Sepoys had to bite them open before loading.
182.tq: Identify the religious implication of the practical loading procedure.
xs: The cartridges were believed to contain **cow and pig fat** and had to be **bitten** open — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Cow** fat offended **Hindus**; **pig** fat offended **Muslims**.
xa: They were read as proof of a **colonial-missionary plot** to force conversion.
Rumours also spoke of **bone dust** in Company flour.

182.s: On which date did the Meerut rising of the Revolt of 1857 begin?
182.x: The Meerut rising began on 10 May 1857; Mangal Pandey's action at Barrackpore was on 29 March and the 19th Native Infantry refused at Berhampur in February 1857.
xa: Mangal Pandey was hanged on **8 April 1857**.
**9 May**: **85** sepoys of the **3rd Cavalry** sentenced to **10 years**.
**11-12 May**: rebels reach **Delhi**.

182.s: What immediately preceded the Meerut rising of 10 May 1857?
o: The proclamation of Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan
The sentencing of 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry to ten years’ imprisonment
The disbandment of Mangal Pandey’s regiment
The refusal of the 19th Native Infantry to use the rifle
182.x: On 9 May 1857, 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut were sentenced to ten years. The rising followed on 10 May, when officers were shot and imprisoned comrades were freed.
182.tq: Identify the immediately preceding event rather than the later consequence.
xs: On **9 May 1857**, **85** sepoys of the **3rd Native Cavalry** were sentenced to **10 years** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The rising followed on **10 May**: officers shot, comrades freed, **"Delhi Chalo"**.
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed only after it (**11-12 May**); the other events were earlier.
xa: Mangal Pandey's regiment was disbanded on **8 April 1857**.
**19th NI** refused the cartridges at **Berhampur** in **February 1857**.

182.s: The rebels who reached Delhi on 11–12 May 1857 proclaimed whom as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan?
182.x: After reaching Delhi, the rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan on 11–12 May 1857.
182.tq: Match the political title with the associated leader.
xs: Rebels reaching Delhi (**11-12 May 1857**) proclaimed **Bahadur Shah II** **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Kunwar Singh** was at Jagdishpur; **Wajid Ali Shah** had been deposed in **1856**; **Nana Sahib** was at Kanpur.
xa: They came from the **Meerut rising** (**10 May**) with the cry **"Delhi Chalo"**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar's successors were to lose the **Red Fort** and **royal title**.

182.s: When did the 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur refuse the new cartridges?
182.x: The Berhampur refusal came in February 1857; Vellore was July 1806, the Barrackpore mutiny November 1824 and Mangal Pandey's attack 29 March 1857.

182.s: Which weapon did the Enfield rifle introduced in December 1856 replace?
182.x: The Enfield rifle replaced the Brown Bess musket; training was at Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot.

182.s: Besides the greased cartridges, with what did a rumour before 1857 say the Company's flour was mixed?
182.x: A rumour spread that bone dust was mixed in Company flour.

182.s: To which regiment did Mangal Pandey belong?
182.x: Mangal Pandey was of the 34th Bengal NI; the 47th NI mutinied at Barrackpore in 1824.

182.s: On which date was Mangal Pandey hanged?
182.x: He attacked Lt Baugh on 29 March and was hanged on 8 April 1857.

182.s: At which of the following places were sepoys trained in the use of the new Enfield rifle?
182.x: Training in the Enfield rifle, introduced in December 1856, was given at Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot.

182.s: Which were the symbols of the Revolt of 1857?
182.x: The lotus and the chapati were the symbols of the Revolt of 1857.

182.s: At the time of revolt of 1857, approximately how many sepoys were in the British Army in India (Choose nearest figure)?
182.src: Assistant Director of Fisheries in A.P. Fisheries Service 20
182.x: On the eve of the revolt the Company had about 2,32,000 Indian sepoys and about 45,000 Europeans (PMF: Indians about 86% of the army).

182.s: What was the first trigger for the Revolt of 1857?
182.x: The revolt was first triggered by the discontent of the sepoys (greased cartridges); lapse, Awadh and civilian grievances widened it later.

182.s: Which of the following was not a reason for making the sepoys of the East India Company rebellious?
o: The efforts of the officers of the company to spread
The order to the sepoys to travel on ships
182.x: Fear of conversion, the order to serve overseas and the stoppage of bhatta angered the sepoys; the inefficiency of officers was not a cause.

182.s: The largest number of soldiers participated in the Struggle of 1857 came from –
182.x: Most rebel sepoys came from Oudh (Awadh), the 'nursery of the Bengal Army' – over 75,000 of them.

182.s: The revolt of 1857 was by?
182.x: The revolt began as a mutiny of the sepoys; landlords and farmers joined later.

182.s: Which of the following has started the revolt of 1857?
182.x: Sepoys started the revolt (Barrackpore, Meerut); zamindars, peasants and others joined later.

182.s:
Which of the following were/was among the grievances that stimulated the Sepoys of the East India Company to rebel?

A. Racial discrimination

B. Caste and religious sentiments

C. Reduction in the allowances

D. Annexation of Awadh
Choose the correct answer from the codes given below
182.x: All four – racial discrimination, caste and religious sentiments (greased cartridges, overseas service), reduced allowances (batta) and the annexation of Awadh, home of many Bengal Army sepoys – stimulated the sepoys.

182.s: The General Service Enlistment Act, 1856 was passed under which Governor-General?
182.x: The Act was Canning's (1856); it required recruits to serve anywhere, including overseas, which orthodox Hindu sepoys feared would cost them caste.
xa: The order to travel by ship **was** a cause (BPSC key).
Earlier: **Barrackpore 1824** — refusal to go to **Burma by sea**.

182.s: What was the 'bhatta' paid to sepoys before 1857?
182.x: Bhatta was the foreign service allowance; it was withdrawn for service in Sindh and Punjab once they became British territory.
xa: **Bhatta mutinies** of the **1840s**: **34th NI 1844**, **66th NI 1849-50**.
Stopping of bhatta **was** a cause (BPSC **2018** key).

182.s: What was the highest rank to which an Indian sepoy could ordinarily rise in the pre-1857 army?
182.x: Racial discrimination restricted the highest rank ordinarily attainable by an Indian soldier to Subedar.
182.tq: Test the exact promotion ceiling rather than general discrimination.
xs: An Indian could rise **no higher than Subedar** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This was part of the **racial discrimination** in pay and promotion.
xa: **APPSC-GS 2023** keyed the Subedar ceiling as correct.
Sepoys got **lower pay** than British soldiers and faced **racial contempt**.
Indians were also shut out of **high civil and military posts**.

182.s: What was the approximate ratio of Indian sepoys to European soldiers in India on the eve of the Revolt of 1857?
182.x: There were about 2.3 lakh Indian sepoys and 45,000 European soldiers, giving an approximate ratio of 5:1.
182.tq: Convert the supplied troop figures into the approximate ratio.
xs: About **2.3 lakh sepoys to 45,000 Europeans** — roughly **5:1** — so option **(4)** is correct.
So sepoys far outnumbered Europeans; ratios like **2:1** or **3:1** understate the gap.
xa: Europeans had been drawn off for the **Crimean and Persian wars**.
**Awadh** was the **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**.

182.s: The expression “peasants in uniform” referred to the fact that the sepoys:
o: Were recruited only from European farming communities
Were trained exclusively in agricultural work
Received land grants instead of salaries
Carried rural and village grievances into the army
182.x: The sepoys were largely drawn from rural communities, so their grievances reflected those of the villages from which they came.
182.tq: Translate a descriptive phrase into its historical implication.
xs: **"Peasants in uniform"**: sepoys **carried rural and village grievances into the army** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Their grievances **mirrored the village's**.
xa: Peasants suffered **heavy land revenue**, **debt** and loss of land to **moneylenders**.
**Awadh** = **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**.

182.s: For sepoys serving in which areas was bhatta, the foreign service allowance, stopped?
182.x: Bhatta was withdrawn for service in Sindh and Punjab, which had become British territory.

182.s: Which region was called the 'nursery of the Bengal Army'?
182.x: Awadh supplied over 75,000 sepoys and was called the nursery of the Bengal Army.

182.s: On the eve of 1857, European troops in India were reduced because they were drawn off for which wars?
182.x: Europeans were drawn off for the Crimean and Persian wars, leaving about 45,000 against 2.3 lakh sepoys.

182.s: Which of the following was NOT a military grievance of the Indian sepoys mentioned in relation to the Revolt of 1857?
o: The ceiling of promotion at the rank of Subedar
182.x: Inefficiency of officers was identified as not being a cause of sepoy anger. Lower pay, racial contempt and the Subedar ceiling were genuine grievances.
182.tq: Find the one item expressly excluded from the list of grievances.
xs: **Inefficiency of officers** was **not** a cause — so option **(3)** is the answer (**BPSC 2018** key).
**Lower pay** than British soldiers, **racial contempt** and the **Subedar** ceiling were real grievances.
xa: **APPSC-GS 2023**: Subedar ceiling + greased cartridges both correct.
Missionary pressure, the order to travel by ship and stopping of **bhatta** **were** causes.

182.s: The Vellore mutiny of 1806 was chiefly triggered by which of the following measures?
o: Introduction of a new dress code and prohibition of caste marks and earrings
Refusal to cross the sea to Burma
Refusal to use the new rifle cartridges
182.x: The new dress code, including a turban with a leather cockade and restrictions on caste marks and earrings, caused resentment among the sepoys at Vellore.
182.tq: Distinguish the cause attached to a specific mutiny.
xs: **Vellore (July 1806)** was triggered by a **new dress code** — turban with **leather cockade**, ban on **caste marks and earrings** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Burma by sea** = **Barrackpore 1824**; **bhatta** = **1840s**; cartridges = **1857**.
xa: **Tipu's sons** were lodged in the Vellore fort.
UPPSC match key: **Vellore = July 1806**; **Barrackpur = Nov 1824**; **Santhal = 1855-56**.

182.s: What did the sepoys refuse to do in the Barrackpore mutiny of November 1824?
182.x: The 47th Native Infantry at Barrackpore refused to go to Burma by sea during the First Anglo-Burmese War.
xs: The **47th NI** at Barrackpore (**November 1824**) refused to **go to Burma by sea** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It came during the **First Anglo-Burmese War**.
xa: ⚠ **Barrackpore 1824** (47th NI, Burma) ≠ **Barrackpore 1857** (**Mangal Pandey**, 34th Bengal NI).
**38th NI (1852)** also refused to go to **Burma**.

182.s: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 is distinguished from the mutinies listed in the context of the 1857 uprising because it was—
o: the first mutiny of the 34th Native Infantry
a civil revolt rather than a sepoy revolt
an uprising caused by the new cartridges
a military revolt over sea service
182.x: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 was a civil revolt and not a sepoy mutiny.
182.tq: Separate a civil revolt from a military mutiny.
xs: The **Santhal revolt (1855-56)** was a **civil revolt, not a sepoy revolt** — so option **(2)** is correct.

182.s: Which of the following was an administrative cause of resentment before the Revolt of 1857?
o: Exclusion of Indians from high civil and military posts
Rapid and inexpensive justice for all social groups
Abolition of corruption in lower courts
Admission of Indians to all high civil and military posts
182.x: Indians were excluded from high civil and military posts, producing resentment against the colonial administrative structure.
xs: Indians were **excluded from high civil and military posts** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Justice was in fact **slow and costly**, and **corruption** was rampant in lower courts, so options 2 and 3 are wrong.
xa: Corruption was rampant in **lower courts and police**; justice **favoured the rich**.
Annexations threw thousands of **officials, retainers and soldiers** of princely courts out of work.
In the army an Indian could rise **no higher than Subedar**.

182.s: What was a major consequence of the high and rigid land revenue demand on peasants?
o: They became independent of moneylenders and traders
They were driven into debt and lost land to moneylenders and traders
They were exempted from commercial cultivation
182.x: The heavy revenue burden pushed peasants into debt, often resulting in the loss of their land to moneylenders and traders.
182.tq: Follow the economic cause to its immediate social consequence.
xs: **Heavy, rigid land revenue** drove peasants into **debt**, and they **lost land to moneylenders and traders** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Revenue was collected rigidly under **Permanent/Zamindari**, **Ryotwari** and **Mahalwari** settlements.
xa: **Commercialisation** forced **cash crops** under high taxes.
Sepoys were **"peasants in uniform"** — they carried these rural grievances into the army.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** + **drain of wealth**.

182.s: Where was the Inam Commission of 1852, which confiscated about 20,000 estates whose owners could not show title, set up?
182.x: The Inam Commission (1852) worked in Bombay, not Madras, and confiscated some 20,000 estates lacking title.
xa: ⚠ **21,000** = taluqdars of Awadh (**1856**); **20,000** = Inam Commission estates (**1852**).
Result: a **fiercely anti-British landed class**.

182.s: What was the main reason for the ruin of Indian artisans and handicrafts before 1857?
o: The Industrial Revolution reduced the supply of British textiles
Indian handicrafts received increased princely patronage after annexations
British machine-made goods entered duty-free, while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs
British goods were excluded from Indian markets
182.x: After the Industrial Revolution, cheap British machine-made goods, especially textiles, entered India duty-free while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs, causing deindustrialisation. A and D reverse this, and B is wrong because annexations ended princely patronage.
182.tq: Compare unequal trade treatment rather than focusing on only one factor.
xs: **British machine-made goods entered duty-free**, while **Indian goods faced heavy tariffs** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This caused **deindustrialisation**; the Industrial Revolution **increased** cheap British goods, esp. **textiles**.
Annexations **ended** princely patronage, so option 2 is wrong.
xa: **Artisans were ruined** by cheap British goods.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** draining wealth to Britain.

182.s: What do the terms 'absentee sovereignty' and 'drain of wealth' refer to in the context of the causes of 1857?
o: the movement of peasants from villages to princely courts
the transfer of religious authority from temples to courts
the transfer of economic resources from India to Britain
the migration of British officials to Indian villages
182.x: Company rule was seen as 'absentee sovereignty', rule from distant Britain, under which India's wealth was drained to Britain. Both terms describe resources being transferred from India to Britain.
182.tq: Distinguish an economic concept from unrelated administrative or religious processes.
xs: Both terms describe **economic resources transferred from India to Britain** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** (rule from distant Britain) plus a **drain of wealth** to Britain.
xa: Peasants faced **heavy land revenue** and lost land to **moneylenders**.
Artisans were ruined by **duty-free** British goods.

182.s: About how many taluqdars of Awadh were dispossessed under the Summary Settlement of 1856?
182.x: About 21,000 taluqdars lost their estates in 1856; 20,000 is the number of estates taken by the Inam Commission.

182.s: The annexation of princely states became a cause of discontent before the Revolt of 1857 because it—
o: ended the drain of wealth to Britain
created employment for thousands of court officials and soldiers
restored the authority of all displaced rulers
threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work
182.x: Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.
182.tq: Trace the administrative consequence of annexation.
xs: Annexations **threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They did the opposite of creating jobs; and Company rule kept the **drain of wealth** going.
xa: In Awadh (**1856**), the deposition of **Wajid Ali Shah** cost lords, officials, retainers and soldiers their livelihoods.
**Pindaris and irregular soldiers** were also disbanded.
Annexations also ended **princely/court patronage** of artisans.

187.s:

Some keys (and the old app notes): both true, R not the explanation, reading A as 'Andhra was little affected'. Strictly the reason given in A is false, so A as stated is false (NextGen modern level 3 part 1 p.41, p.43).
A is false: Andhra did have local leaders in 1857 – Korukonda Subba Reddy, Dandasena and Sheikh Peer Saheb – and it was little affected because most people stayed loyal and valued the Company's stable rule. R is true: Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula stayed loyal and ordered the conspirators arrested.

187.s: Why did the Revolt of 1857 have only a limited impact in South India?
o: The British had withdrawn their forces from the Deccan before 1857
The rulers of all South Indian states openly supported the revolt

xs: South India's revolts were **local and scattered**, and the **Nizam's loyalty** kept the **Deccan** closed to 1857 — so option **(3)** is correct.
The British had not withdrawn, and southern rulers like the **Nizam** stayed **pro-British**.

preached jihad and prayed for the success of the Mughal Emperor
